entries.question: What is AI?
entries.answer: Machines performing tasks that normally need human intelligence: understanding language, recognising images, making decisions, learning from examples.
entries.summary: Machines performing tasks that normally need human intelligence: understanding language, recognising images, making decisions, learning from examples.

entries.question: What is the difference between AI, Machine Learning and Deep Learning?
entries.answer:
| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| AI | The broad field: machines doing "intelligent" tasks (includes rule-based systems) |
| Machine Learning | A subset of AI: systems **learn patterns from data** instead of being explicitly programmed |
| Deep Learning | A subset of ML: uses **multi-layer neural networks** (vision, speech, LLMs) |
| Generative AI | Deep-learning models that **create** new content |

AI ⊃ ML ⊃ Deep Learning ⊃ (most of) Generative AI.
entries.summary: AI ⊃ ML ⊃ Deep Learning ⊃ (most of) Generative AI.

entries.question: What is Generative AI?
entries.answer: AI that generates new content — text, code, images, audio or video — from a prompt, instead of only classifying or predicting. ChatGPT, Claude and image generators are examples.
entries.summary: AI that generates new content — text, code, images, audio or video — from a prompt, instead of only classifying or predicting. ChatGPT, Claude and image generators are examples.

entries.question: What is an LLM (Large Language Model)?
entries.answer: A deep-learning model (usually a Transformer) trained on very large amounts of text to predict the next token. That simple objective, at scale, lets it answer questions, summarise, translate and write code.
entries.summary: A deep-learning model (usually a Transformer) trained on very large amounts of text to predict the next token. That simple objective, at scale, lets it answer questions, summarise, translate and write code.

entries.question: What is NLP?
entries.answer: Natural Language Processing: the field of making computers understand and produce human language — tokenisation, sentiment analysis, translation, question answering. LLMs are today's dominant NLP technique.
entries.summary: Natural Language Processing: the field of making computers understand and produce human language — tokenisation, sentiment analysis, translation, question answering. LLMs are today's dominant NLP technique.

entries.question: What is a neural network?
entries.answer: A computational model of layers of connected "neurons". Each connection has a weight; training adjusts the weights so the network's outputs match the expected ones. Deep learning means many such layers.
entries.summary: A computational model of layers of connected "neurons". Each connection has a weight; training adjusts the weights so the network's outputs match the expected ones. Deep learning means many such layers.

entries.question: What is the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning?
entries.answer:
| Supervised | Unsupervised |
|---|---|
| Trained on **labelled** data (input + correct answer) | Trained on **unlabelled** data |
| Predicts labels or values | Finds structure: clusters, patterns |
| Spam detection, price prediction | Customer segmentation, anomaly detection |

LLM pre-training is **self-supervised**: the "label" is simply the next token in the text.
entries.summary: LLM pre-training is self-supervised: the "label" is simply the next token in the text.

entries.question: What is ChatGPT (or Claude) based on internally?
entries.answer: **Transformer**-based large language models. The Transformer's **attention** mechanism lets every token weigh every other token in the context. The models are pre-trained on large text corpora, then fine-tuned with instruction data and human feedback (RLHF) to follow instructions and be helpful.
entries.summary: Transformer-based large language models. The Transformer's attention mechanism lets every token weigh every other token in the context. The models are pre-trained on large text corpora, then fine-tuned with instruction data and human feedback (RLHF) to follow instructions and be helpful.

entries.question: How does an LLM work at a high level?
entries.answer:
1. The input text is split into **tokens**. 2. Each token becomes a vector (an **embedding**). 3. Transformer layers use attention to build a representation of the whole context. 4. The model outputs a probability for every possible next token. 5. One token is chosen (influenced by **temperature**), appended, and the process repeats until the answer is complete. ```mermaid flowchart LR T["Text: The cat sat"] --> K["Tokens"] --> E["Embeddings
(vectors)"] E --> L["Transformer layers
(attention over context)"] L --> P["Next-token probabilities
on: 62%, down: 21%, ..."] P --> C["Pick one token
(temperature)"] C -- append and repeat --> K ``` The model doesn't look facts up; it predicts likely text — which is why grounding (RAG) matters.
entries.summary: The input text is split into tokens. Each token becomes a vector (an embedding). Transformer layers use attention to build a representation of the whole context. The model outputs a probability for every possible next token. One token is chosen (influenced by temperature), appended, and the process repeats until the…

entries.question: What is a token?
entries.answer: A unit of text the model processes — a word, part of a word or a punctuation mark. Roughly 1 token ≈ 4 English characters ≈ ¾ of a word. API pricing, rate limits and context windows are measured in tokens.
entries.summary: A unit of text the model processes — a word, part of a word or a punctuation mark. Roughly 1 token ≈ 4 English characters ≈ ¾ of a word. API pricing, rate limits and context windows are measured in tokens.

entries.question: What is a context window?
entries.answer: The maximum number of tokens (prompt + conversation history + retrieved documents + the generated answer) the model can handle in one request. Anything beyond it must be truncated, summarised or retrieved selectively.
entries.summary: The maximum number of tokens (prompt + conversation history + retrieved documents + the generated answer) the model can handle in one request. Anything beyond it must be truncated, summarised or retrieved selectively.

entries.question: What is temperature?
entries.answer: A setting that controls randomness. Low (≈0) → focused, repeatable answers (good for extraction, code, factual Q&A). High (≈1) → more varied, creative output.
entries.summary: A setting that controls randomness. Low (≈0) → focused, repeatable answers (good for extraction, code, factual Q&A). High (≈1) → more varied, creative output.

entries.question: What is hallucination?
entries.answer: When the model produces confident but incorrect or invented information — fake facts, citations or APIs. It happens because the model predicts plausible text rather than checking facts.
entries.summary: When the model produces confident but incorrect or invented information — fake facts, citations or APIs. It happens because the model predicts plausible text rather than checking facts.

entries.question: What is prompt engineering?
entries.answer: Designing instructions that get reliable results: a clear role and task, relevant context, constraints, examples (few-shot) and a required output format such as JSON.
entries.summary: Designing instructions that get reliable results: a clear role and task, relevant context, constraints, examples (few-shot) and a required output format such as JSON.

entries.question: What is fine-tuning?
entries.answer: Further training a pre-trained model on task-specific examples so its **behaviour** changes — a style, format or domain skill. It is costly to maintain and doesn't add up-to-date facts well; RAG is usually the first choice for private knowledge.
entries.summary: Further training a pre-trained model on task-specific examples so its behaviour changes — a style, format or domain skill. It is costly to maintain and doesn't add up-to-date facts well; RAG is usually the first choice for private knowledge.

entries.question: What is RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)?
entries.answer:
Before calling the LLM, the application **retrieves** relevant pieces of its own documents and puts them into the prompt. The model then answers **from that context**, ideally with citations.

```text
Question → embed → vector search → top-k chunks → prompt (question + chunks) → LLM → answer with sources
```
entries.summary: Before calling the LLM, the application retrieves relevant pieces of its own documents and puts them into the prompt. The model then answers from that context, ideally with citations.

codeBlocks.code: Question → embed → vector search → top-k chunks → prompt (question + chunks) → LLM → answer with sources

entries.question: Why do we need RAG?
entries.answer: LLMs don't know your private or recent data and may hallucinate. RAG supplies company documents at query time without retraining, keeps answers current (update the index, not the model), and makes answers traceable to sources.
entries.summary: LLMs don't know your private or recent data and may hallucinate. RAG supplies company documents at query time without retraining, keeps answers current (update the index, not the model), and makes answers traceable to sources.

entries.question: What are embeddings?
entries.answer: Numeric vectors that represent the **meaning** of text (or images). Similar meanings produce vectors that are close together, measured with cosine similarity, for example. "Reset my password" and "I forgot my login" end up near each other.
entries.summary: Numeric vectors that represent the meaning of text (or images). Similar meanings produce vectors that are close together, measured with cosine similarity, for example. "Reset my password" and "I forgot my login" end up near each other.

entries.question: What is a vector database?
entries.answer: A database that stores embeddings and finds the nearest vectors to a query vector quickly (approximate nearest-neighbour indexes such as HNSW). Examples: pgvector, Pinecone, Weaviate, Milvus, Elasticsearch, Redis.
entries.summary: A database that stores embeddings and finds the nearest vectors to a query vector quickly (approximate nearest-neighbour indexes such as HNSW). Examples: pgvector, Pinecone, Weaviate, Milvus, Elasticsearch, Redis.

entries.question: What is semantic search?
entries.answer: Search by **meaning** instead of exact keywords: the query is embedded and compared with document embeddings. Often combined with keyword search (hybrid search) for names and codes.
entries.summary: Search by meaning instead of exact keywords: the query is embedded and compared with document embeddings. Often combined with keyword search (hybrid search) for names and codes.

entries.question: What is the difference between RAG and fine-tuning?
entries.answer:
| | RAG | Fine-tuning |
|---|---|---|
| What changes | The **context** given to the model | The model's **weights** |
| Best for | Private, changing knowledge | Style, format, specialised behaviour |
| Updating knowledge | Re-index documents | Retrain |
| Citations | Natural | Not available |
| Cost | Lower, operational | Higher, training |
entries.summary: What changes: The context given to the model; Best for: Private, changing knowledge; Updating knowledge: Re-index documents; Citations: Natural; Cost: Lower, operational

entries.question: What is chunking?
entries.answer: Splitting documents into smaller pieces (for example 300–800 tokens with some overlap) before embedding them, so retrieval returns focused passages that fit the context window. Chunk size and overlap strongly affect answer quality.
entries.summary: Splitting documents into smaller pieces (for example 300–800 tokens with some overlap) before embedding them, so retrieval returns focused passages that fit the context window. Chunk size and overlap strongly affect answer quality.

entries.question: What is an AI agent?
entries.answer: An AI system that can **reason about a goal, choose tools, act, observe the results and continue** until the task is done — for example, look up an order, check stock and draft a reply.
entries.summary: An AI system that can reason about a goal, choose tools, act, observe the results and continue until the task is done — for example, look up an order, check stock and draft a reply.

entries.question: What is the difference between an LLM and an AI agent?
entries.answer: An LLM produces a response to one prompt. An agent wraps the LLM in a **loop with tools and memory**: it decides which action to take, executes it (API call, database query), feeds the result back to the model, and repeats.
entries.summary: An LLM produces a response to one prompt. An agent wraps the LLM in a loop with tools and memory: it decides which action to take, executes it (API call, database query), feeds the result back to the model, and repeats.

entries.question: What is tool calling (function calling)?
entries.answer: The model returns a structured request to call a function you defined (name plus JSON arguments) instead of plain text. Your application executes it and sends the result back; the model then continues. It is how LLMs reach real systems safely — the application stays in control of what actually runs.
entries.summary: The model returns a structured request to call a function you defined (name plus JSON arguments) instead of plain text. Your application executes it and sends the result back; the model then continues. It is how LLMs reach real systems safely — the application stays in control of what actually runs.

entries.question: What is MCP (Model Context Protocol)?
entries.answer: An open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data sources. An **MCP server** exposes tools, resources and prompts (for example GitHub, a database, internal APIs); any MCP-capable client or agent can use them without a custom integration for each pair.
entries.summary: An open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data sources. An MCP server exposes tools, resources and prompts (for example GitHub, a database, internal APIs); any MCP-capable client or agent can use them without a custom integration for each pair.

entries.question: What is a multi-agent architecture?
entries.answer: Several specialised agents (planner, researcher, coder, reviewer) cooperate on a task, usually coordinated by an orchestrator. It helps with complex work but adds latency, cost and debugging complexity.
entries.summary: Several specialised agents (planner, researcher, coder, reviewer) cooperate on a task, usually coordinated by an orchestrator. It helps with complex work but adds latency, cost and debugging complexity.

entries.question: What is an agentic workflow?
entries.answer:
A workflow in which the AI decides and executes the next steps itself (plan → act → check → adjust) rather than following a fixed sequence — typically with guardrails, limits and human approval for risky actions.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  G[Goal] --> P[Plan next step]
  P --> A["Act: call a tool / API"]
  A --> C{Check result: done?}
  C -- no, adjust --> P
  C -- yes --> D[Answer]
  A -. risky action .-> H[Human approval]
```

entries.question: How would you integrate an LLM API (OpenAI, Claude…) into Spring Boot?
entries.summary: Use Spring AI: add the starter for your provider, put the API key in configuration (from an environment variable or a secrets manager, never in code), and inject a ChatClient.

codeBlocks.code: spring.ai.openai.api-key=${OPENAI_API_KEY}

entries.question: How would you build an AI chatbot with Spring Boot and Angular?
entries.answer:
- **Angular:** chat UI, sends the message plus a conversation id, renders the streamed answer (Markdown, code blocks).
- **Spring Boot:** authenticates the user, loads recent conversation history, optionally retrieves documents (RAG), calls the LLM through Spring AI, streams the answer back over Server-Sent Events, stores the conversation.
- **Cross-cutting:** rate limiting per user, logging of token usage, content filtering, timeouts and fallbacks.

entries.question: How would you implement RAG using company documents in Spring Boot?
entries.answer:
**Ingestion (offline):** read documents → split into chunks → create embeddings → store in a vector store.
**Query time:** retrieve the top-k chunks for the question → build a prompt with them → ask the LLM to answer only from them and cite sources.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Ingest["Ingestion (offline)"]
    direction LR
    D[Documents] --> S[Split into chunks] --> E1[Embed] --> V[(Vector store)]
  end
  subgraph Ask["Query time"]
    direction LR
    Q[Question] --> E2[Embed] --> R["Find top-k similar chunks"]
    R --> P["Prompt = question + chunks"] --> L[LLM] --> A[Answer with sources]
  end
  V --> R
```

```java
// Ingestion
List<Document> chunks = new TokenTextSplitter().apply(documents);
vectorStore.add(chunks);                    // embeds and stores each chunk

// Question answering
List<Document> context = vectorStore.similaritySearch(
    SearchRequest.builder().query(question).topK(5).build());

String sources = context.stream().map(Document::getText).collect(Collectors.joining("\n---\n"));
String answer = chatClient.prompt()
    .system("Answer only from the sources below. If they don't contain the answer, say so.\n" + sources)
    .user(question)
    .call()
    .content();
```

Also apply access control to retrieval: users must only retrieve documents they are allowed to read.
entries.summary: Ingestion (offline): read documents → split into chunks → create embeddings → store in a vector store. Query time: retrieve the top-k chunks for the question → build a prompt with them → ask the LLM to answer only from them and cite sources.

entries.question: How would you secure sensitive data sent to an external LLM?
entries.answer:
- Send only what's needed; **mask or remove PII** and secrets before the call.
- Use providers and plans with data-processing agreements and no training on your data; choose a region if required.
- Enforce authorization before retrieval, so the model never sees documents the user can't access.
- Keep API keys in a secrets manager; log prompts carefully (redacted).
- For highly sensitive data, use a self-hosted or private-cloud model.

Use providers and plans with data-processing agreements and no training on your data; choose a region if required. entries.question: How would you handle LLM API rate limits and token costs?
entries.answer:
- Retry `429` responses with exponential backoff and jitter (e.g. Resilience4j), with a cap.
- Rate-limit per user and per tenant; queue non-urgent work.
- Reduce tokens: trim history, summarise long conversations, retrieve fewer and smaller chunks, set `max_tokens`.
- Use smaller, cheaper models for simple tasks; use prompt caching where the provider supports it.
- Track token usage per feature and user; alert on budgets.

entries.question: How would you implement streaming AI responses?
entries.summary: Stream tokens as they are generated, so users see the answer start in about a second instead of waiting for the whole response.

entries.question: How would you reduce hallucinations?
entries.answer: Ground answers with RAG and require citations; instruct the model to say "I don't know" when the context lacks the answer; use low temperature; validate outputs (schemas, business rules, checking cited sources exist); use confidence thresholds or a second verification pass; add human review for high-risk answers.
entries.summary: Ground answers with RAG and require citations; instruct the model to say "I don't know" when the context lacks the answer; use low temperature; validate outputs (schemas, business rules, checking cited sources exist); use confidence thresholds or a second verification pass; add human review for high-risk answers.

entries.question: How would you evaluate the accuracy of AI-generated answers?
entries.answer: Build a **test set** of real questions with expected answers or sources. Measure retrieval quality (did the right chunks come back?), answer correctness and faithfulness to sources (human review or an LLM-as-judge with a rubric), and track user feedback. Run the evaluation on every prompt, model or chunking change, like regression tests.

entries.question: How would you implement AI response caching?
entries.answer:
- **Exact cache:** key = hash of (model, prompt, parameters) → stored answer in Redis with a TTL.
- **Semantic cache:** embed the question and reuse an answer when a previous question is very similar.
- Don't cache personalised or permission-dependent answers across users; invalidate when the source documents change.

Semantic cache: embed the question and reuse an answer when a previous question is very similar. Don't cache personalised or permission-dependent answers across users; invalidate when the source documents change.

entries.question: How would you design fallbacks if the LLM provider is unavailable?
entries.answer: Set timeouts, use a circuit breaker (Resilience4j), and on failure fall back to a secondary provider or model, a cached answer, or a non-AI path (search results, "try again later"). Show a clear message and never block core business flows on the LLM.
entries.summary: Set timeouts, use a circuit breaker (Resilience4j), and on failure fall back to a secondary provider or model, a cached answer, or a non-AI path (search results, "try again later"). Show a clear message and never block core business flows on the LLM.

entries.question: An LLM API takes 20 seconds to respond. How would you improve the user experience?
entries.answer: Stream the response; process long tasks asynchronously with progress updates; cache frequent answers; use a faster or smaller model where quality allows; shorten prompts and retrieved context; run independent calls in parallel.
entries.summary: Stream the response; process long tasks asynchronously with progress updates; cache frequent answers; use a faster or smaller model where quality allows; shorten prompts and retrieved context; run independent calls in parallel.

entries.question: The AI gives incorrect answers about financial information. How would you minimise this?
entries.answer: Use RAG over authoritative data, require source citations, compute numbers in code from the database rather than letting the model calculate, validate outputs against business rules, use confidence thresholds, and route uncertain or high-impact answers to human review.
entries.summary: Use RAG over authoritative data, require source citations, compute numbers in code from the database rather than letting the model calculate, validate outputs against business rules, use confidence thresholds, and route uncertain or high-impact answers to human review.

entries.question: How would you prevent prompt injection attacks?
entries.answer: Treat all user input and retrieved content as **data, not instructions**: keep system instructions separate, delimit untrusted content, give tools least-privilege permissions, require confirmation for sensitive actions, validate and filter outputs, and never let model output directly run commands or queries without checks.
entries.summary: Treat all user input and retrieved content as data, not instructions: keep system instructions separate, delimit untrusted content, give tools least-privilege permissions, require confirmation for sensitive actions, validate and filter outputs, and never let model output directly run commands or queries without checks.

entries.question: What are Core Web Vitals?
entries.answer:
Three numbers Google uses to measure **real user experience** (and as a search ranking signal):

| Metric | Measures | Good | Poor |
|---|---|---|---|
| **LCP** — Largest Contentful Paint | **Loading:** when the main content appears | ≤ 2.5 s | > 4 s |
| **INP** — Interaction to Next Paint | **Responsiveness:** delay after a click/tap/key until the screen updates | ≤ 200 ms | > 500 ms |
| **CLS** — Cumulative Layout Shift | **Visual stability:** how much the page jumps around | ≤ 0.1 | > 0.25 |

A page "passes" when **75% of real visits** are in the good range.

**Measure them:** Chrome DevTools / Lighthouse (lab), PageSpeed Insights and Search Console (real users), or the `web-vitals` JS library in your own analytics.
entries.summary: Three numbers Google uses to measure real user experience (and as a search ranking signal):

entries.question: What happened to FID?
entries.answer: ↪ INP replaced FID (First Input Delay) in March 2024. FID only measured the first interaction's delay; INP looks at all interactions and the full time until the screen updates.
entries.summary: INP replaced FID (First Input Delay) in March 2024. FID only measured the first interaction's delay; INP looks at all interactions and the full time until the screen updates.

entries.question: What is Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) and how do you improve it?
entries.answer: LCP is when the **largest visible element** (usually the hero image or main heading) finishes rendering. Good: **≤ 2.5 s**. **Improve it:** - Load the hero image **early and first**: `fetchpriority="high"`, never `loading="lazy"` on it. - Make it **small**: right size, WebP/AVIF, served from a CDN. - Reduce **render-blocking** CSS/JS in the ``. - Speed up the server response (caching, CDN, SSR/static HTML). ```html ```
entries.summary: LCP is when the largest visible element (usually the hero image or main heading) finishes rendering. Good: ≤ 2.5 s.

entries.question: How to reduce CLS?
entries.answer:
CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) grows when content **moves after it appears** — e.g. an image loads and pushes text down while you're reading or about to tap. Fix it by **reserving space** before things load. - Give images and videos `width` + `height` (or `aspect-ratio`). - Reserve space for ads, embeds and banners (`min-height`). - Don't insert content **above** existing content — show toasts and banners as overlays. - Load fonts with `font-display: swap` plus a similar fallback font (or `size-adjust`) so text doesn't jump. ```html
``` > 💡 Changes within 500 ms after a user's click don't count — expected movement (opening an accordion) is fine.
entries.summary: CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) grows when content moves after it appears — e.g. an image loads and pushes text down while you're reading or about to tap. Fix it by reserving space before things load.

entries.question: What is INP and how do you improve it?
entries.answer:
INP (Interaction to Next Paint) is the time from a user's **click, tap or key press** until the browser **paints the result**. Good: **≤ 200 ms**. It's slow when the **main thread is busy** with JavaScript.

**Improve it:**

- Break long tasks (> 50 ms) into smaller pieces and **yield** to the browser.
- Update the UI first, do heavy work after (or in a Web Worker).
- Debounce expensive handlers (search as you type).
- Avoid huge DOM updates; virtualise long lists.

```js
button.addEventListener("click", async () => {
  showSpinner();                                   // 1. quick visual feedback
  await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 0));        // 2. let the browser paint it
  doHeavyWork();                                   // 3. then the slow part
});
```

Newer browsers also offer `await scheduler.yield()` for step 2.
entries.summary: INP (Interaction to Next Paint) is the time from a user's click, tap or key press until the browser paints the result. Good: ≤ 200 ms. It's slow when the main thread is busy with JavaScript.

entries.question: How to reduce JS main-thread blocking time?
entries.summary: The browser's main thread does JavaScript and layout and painting. Long JS tasks freeze the page. Ways to reduce them:

codeBlocks.code: <script src="/non-critical.js" defer></script>

keywords: move heavy work off the main thread

entries.question: How to implement image optimization?
entries.answer: Send the **smallest image that still looks right**: - **Modern formats:** AVIF / WebP (often 30–50% smaller than JPEG). - **Right size per screen:** `srcset` + `sizes`, so phones don't download desktop images. - **Lazy-load** images below the fold (`loading="lazy"`) — but never the LCP image. - Always set `width`/`height` (prevents CLS) and serve from a **CDN**. ```html ``` The browser picks the first format it supports, and the best width for the screen.

entries.question: Lazy loading non-critical JS.
entries.summary: Don't download code until it's needed: on user action, when it scrolls into view, or when the browser is idle. Use dynamic import(), which bundlers turn into a separate chunk.

codeBlocks.code:
<button id="open-chat">Open Chat</button>

<script type="module">
  // Load the chat widget only when someone clicks
  document.getElementById("open-chat").addEventListener("click", async () => {
    const { initChatWidget } = await import("./chat-widget.js");
    initChatWidget();
  });

  // Load analytics when the browser has nothing else to do
  if ("requestIdleCallback" in window) {
    requestIdleCallback(() => import("./analytics.js"));
  }
</script>

entries.question: What are the main AWS Compute services (EC2, Lambda, Auto Scaling, Elastic Beanstalk, ECS, EKS, Fargate)?
entries.answer:
**Core Compute Services (VERY IMPORTANT)**

| Service                          | Explanation                                                                                                        |
| -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Amazon EC2**                   | Virtual servers in the cloud. You choose instance type, OS, storage, and network. Used for full control workloads. |
| **EC2 Auto Scaling**             | Automatically adds or removes EC2 instances based on demand to maintain performance and reduce cost.               |
| **Elastic Load Balancing (ELB)** | Distributes incoming traffic across multiple targets (EC2, containers, IPs) to improve availability.               |
| **AWS Lambda**                   | Serverless compute. Run code without managing servers. Pay only for execution time.                                |
| **AWS Elastic Beanstalk**        | Platform as a Service (PaaS) for deploying applications without managing infrastructure.                           |
| **Amazon Lightsail**             | Simplified compute for small apps, websites, or beginners with predictable pricing.                                |

**Container & Modern Compute (High-Level Awareness)**

| Service            | Explanation                                                                            |
| ------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Amazon ECS**     | Managed container orchestration for Docker containers.                                 |
| **Amazon EKS**     | Managed Kubernetes service.                                                            |
| **AWS Fargate**    | Serverless compute engine for containers (used with ECS/EKS).                          |
| **AWS App Runner** | Fully managed service to run containerized web apps without infrastructure management. |

**Batch & Specialized Compute (Basic Recognition Only)**

| Service               | Explanation                                                      |
| --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **AWS Batch**         | Runs batch computing jobs at any scale without managing servers. |
| **EC2 Image Builder** | Automates creation of secure VM images (AMI).                    |

**Hybrid & Edge Compute (Conceptual Awareness)**

| Service                 | Explanation                                          |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| **AWS Outposts**        | AWS infrastructure on-premises (hybrid cloud).       |
| **AWS Wavelength**      | Ultra-low latency compute for 5G applications.       |
| **VMware Cloud on AWS** | Run VMware workloads directly on AWS infrastructure. |

![AWS_Compute Image](/src/assets/aws-compute.png)

entries.question: AWS Compute: which service fits each scenario?
entries.answer:

2️⃣ An application must automatically increase or decrease EC2 instances based on traffic → **Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling**

3️⃣ Incoming traffic must be distributed across multiple EC2 instances → **Elastic Load Balancing (ELB)**

5️⃣ A startup wants the easiest way to deploy a small web application with minimal configuration → **Amazon Lightsail**

7️⃣ Containers must be run without managing the underlying servers → **AWS Fargate**

8️⃣ A company wants to run Docker containers using AWS-managed orchestration → **Amazon ECS**

9️⃣ An organization needs a managed Kubernetes service → **Amazon EKS**

🔟 Large-scale batch jobs must be processed efficiently without manual resource management → **AWS Batch**

1️⃣1️⃣ A developer wants to run microservices using containers with AWS handling scheduling and scaling → **Amazon ECS**

1️⃣2️⃣ Compute workloads must run only when an event occurs and stop automatically → **AWS Lambda**

1️⃣3️⃣ A business wants to deploy AWS infrastructure inside its on-premises data center → **AWS Outposts**

1️⃣4️⃣ A low-latency application must be delivered to 5G mobile devices → **AWS Wavelength**

1️⃣5️⃣ A company wants to migrate VMware workloads to AWS without re-architecting → **VMware Cloud on AWS**

1️⃣6️⃣ A web application must scale automatically and remain highly available → **Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling**

1️⃣7️⃣ Developers want a managed platform to upload code and let AWS handle capacity planning → **AWS Elastic Beanstalk**

1️⃣8️⃣ A containerized application must run with no cluster or server management → **AWS Fargate**

entries.question: What are the main AWS Storage services (S3, Glacier, EBS, EFS, FSx)?
entries.answer:
| **Service**                          | **Storage Type**        | **Explanation**                                                                                                                                                                  |
| ------------------------------------ | ----------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Amazon S3**                        | Object Storage          | Scalable object storage used to store files such as images, videos, backups, logs, and static website content. Data is stored as objects in buckets and accessed via HTTP/HTTPS. |
| **Amazon S3 Glacier**                | Archival Object Storage | Low-cost storage for long-term data archiving where data is accessed infrequently. Retrieval takes minutes to hours depending on the retrieval option.                           |
| **Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive**   | Archival Object Storage | Lowest-cost AWS storage option designed for long-term data retention (years). Data retrieval usually takes hours.                                                                |
| **Amazon EBS (Elastic Block Store)** | Block Storage           | Persistent block-level storage used with EC2 instances. Data remains even after EC2 is stopped and is typically used for OS disks or databases.                                  |
| **Amazon EFS (Elastic File System)** | File Storage            | Fully managed, scalable file system that can be mounted on multiple EC2 instances simultaneously. Commonly used for shared file systems.                                         |
| **Amazon FSx**                       | File Storage            | Managed file systems for specific workloads such as Windows File Server or high-performance computing. Cloud Practitioner only requires recognition, not deep details.           |
| **AWS Storage Gateway**              | Hybrid Storage          | Connects on-premises environments with AWS cloud storage, allowing local applications to store data in AWS seamlessly.                                                           |
| **AWS Backup**                       | Backup Service          | Centralized service to automate and manage backups across AWS services like EBS, EFS, RDS, and DynamoDB.                                                                         |

![AWS_Storage Image](/src/assets/aws-storage.png)
entries.summary: Amazon S3: Object Storage; Amazon S3 Glacier: Archival Object Storage; Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive: Archival Object Storage; Amazon EBS (Elastic Block Store): Block Storage; Amazon EFS (Elastic File System): File Storage; Amazon FSx: File Storage; AWS Storage Gateway: Hybrid Storage; AWS Backup: Backup Service

entries.question: What are the main AWS Networking & Content Delivery services (VPC, Route 53, CloudFront, API Gateway)?
entries.answer:
![AWS_DNS Image](/src/assets/aws-dns.png)

| **Service**                      | **Explanation**                                                                                                                                     |
| -------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Amazon VPC**                   | A logically isolated virtual network in AWS. Used to launch AWS resources (EC2, RDS, etc.) in a private, controlled network with your own IP ranges |
| **Subnets**                      | A segmented range of IPs inside a VPC. Used to separate resources (public vs private) across Availability Zones                                     |
| **Internet Gateway (IGW)**       | A gateway that allows VPC resources to access the internet. Required for public subnets so instances can send/receive internet traffic              |
| **NAT Gateway**                  | Allows private subnet resources to access the internet. Used when instances must download updates but must NOT be publicly accessible               |
| **Route Tables**                 | Rules that control traffic routing in a VPC. Determines where network traffic is directed (IGW, NAT, VPC peering, etc.)                             |
| **Security Groups**              | Virtual firewall at the instance level. Controls inbound and outbound traffic (stateful)                                                            |
| **Network ACL (NACL)**           | Firewall at the subnet level. Provides an extra layer of security (stateless)                                                                       |
| **Elastic Load Balancing (ELB)** | Distributes incoming traffic across multiple targets. Improves availability and fault tolerance (ALB, NLB – no deep config needed for exam)         |
| **Amazon Route 53**              | Highly available DNS (Domain Name System) service. Routes users to applications using domain names and routing policies                             |
| **Amazon CloudFront**            | Content Delivery Network (CDN). Delivers content (images, videos, APIs) with low latency using edge locations                                       |
| **AWS Direct Connect**           | Dedicated private connection from on-premises to AWS. Used for consistent network performance and lower latency (enterprise use case)               |
| **Site-to-Site VPN**             | Encrypted tunnel between on-prem and AWS. Used for hybrid cloud connectivity over the public internet                                               |
| **AWS Global Accelerator**       | Improves availability and performance using AWS global network. Routes traffic to the nearest healthy endpoint using static IPs                     |
| **Amazon API Gateway**           | Managed service to create, publish, and secure APIs. Acts as a front door for applications (often used with Lambda)                                 |

![AWS_Network Image](/src/assets/aws-network.png)

entries.question: What are the main AWS Security, Identity & Compliance services (IAM, KMS, Shield, WAF, GuardDuty)?
entries.answer:
| **Service**                                  | **Explanation**                                                                                                                  |
| -------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)** | Core AWS service to **manage users, groups, roles, and permissions**. Uses policies written in JSON to define _who can do what_. |
| **IAM Identity Center (SSO)**                | Centralized **single sign-on (SSO)** service to manage access across **multiple AWS accounts and applications**.                 |
| **Amazon Cognito**                           | Provides **user sign-up, sign-in, and authentication** for web and mobile apps. Used for **application users**, not AWS admins.  |
| **AWS Organizations**                        | Helps manage **multiple AWS accounts** centrally, apply **Service Control Policies (SCPs)**, and consolidate billing.            |
| **AWS Key Management Service (KMS)**         | Managed service to **create, manage, and control encryption keys** used to encrypt data across AWS services.                     |
| **AWS Secrets Manager**                      | Securely **stores and rotates secrets** like database passwords, API keys, and tokens.                                           |
| **AWS Certificate Manager (ACM)**            | Manages **SSL/TLS certificates** for services like ALB, CloudFront, and API Gateway.                                             |
| **AWS Shield**                               | Provides **DDoS protection**. Shield Standard is automatic and free; Shield Advanced offers enhanced protection.                 |
| **AWS Web Application Firewall (WAF)**       | Protects web applications from **common web exploits** like SQL injection and XSS attacks.                                       |
| **Amazon GuardDuty**                         | **Threat detection service** that continuously monitors AWS accounts for malicious activity using ML and logs.                   |
| **Amazon Inspector**                         | **Automated security assessment** service that scans EC2 and container workloads for vulnerabilities.                            |
| **Amazon Macie**                             | Uses ML to **discover and protect sensitive data** (like PII) stored in Amazon S3️⃣                                               |
| **AWS Security Hub**                         | Central dashboard that **aggregates security findings** from multiple AWS security services.                                     |
| **AWS Artifact**                             | Provides **on-demand access to compliance reports** and agreements (SOC, ISO, PCI).                                              |
| **AWS CloudTrail**                           | Records **all API calls and account activity** for auditing and compliance.                                                      |

entries.answer:

| **Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS)**        | A fully managed message queue service that decouples application components by allowing them to send, store, and receive messages asynchronously. | **Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS)** | A fully managed pub/sub messaging service used to send messages or notifications to multiple subscribers at once. SNS supports fan-out to services like SQS, Lambda, HTTP endpoints, email, SMS, and mobile push notifications.                                            |
| **Amazon EventBridge**                       | A serverless event bus that enables event-driven architectures by routing events from AWS services, SaaS applications, or custom applications to targets like Lambda. It allows loosely coupled systems to react to events in real time.                                   |
| **AWS Step Functions**                       | A serverless orchestration service that coordinates multiple AWS services into visual workflows. It is commonly used to build multi-step applications by managing execution order, retries, error handling, and state tracking.                                            |
| **Amazon MQ**                                | A managed message broker service for Apache ActiveMQ and RabbitMQ. It is mainly used when migrating existing applications that rely on traditional message brokers and standard protocols like JMS, AMQP, or MQTT.                                                         |
| **Amazon Simple Workflow Service (SWF)**     | A service that helps coordinate long-running background jobs with multiple steps. It tracks task states and execution progress, making it suitable for workflows that take longer than typical request-response operations.                                                |

entries.question: What is Docker and why is it used?
entries.answer:
Docker packages an application **with everything it needs** (runtime, libraries, config) into a **container** that runs the same way on any machine. ```mermaid flowchart LR D[Dockerfile] -- docker build --> I[Image
app + Java + libraries] I --> L[Laptop container] I --> T[Test container] I --> P[Production container] ``` - **Problem it solves:** "It works on my machine" — different Java versions, missing libraries, different OS settings between laptops, test and production. - **Why teams prefer it:** the same image goes from laptop → test → production, starts in seconds, and many containers share one server. ```bash docker run -p 8080:8080 myapp:1.0 # same result on every machine ```
entries.summary: Docker packages an application with everything it needs (runtime, libraries, config) into a container that runs the same way on any machine.

entries.question: What is the difference between Docker and a Virtual Machine?
entries.answer:
| Virtual machine | Docker container |
|---|---|
| Runs a **full guest operating system** on virtual hardware | **Shares the host's OS kernel**; contains only the app and its libraries |
| Size in GBs, boots in minutes | Size in MBs, starts in seconds |
| Strong isolation | Lighter isolation (process level) |
| A few VMs per server | Dozens or hundreds of containers per server |

Containers start fast because there's **no operating system to boot** — starting one is like starting a process.
entries.summary: Containers start fast because there's no operating system to boot — starting one is like starting a process.

entries.question: What is a Docker image?
entries.answer:
An image is a **read-only template** for creating containers — like a class, while a container is an object.

- **Contains:** a base OS layer (e.g. a slim Linux), the runtime (JRE), your app (JAR), and settings (ports, start command).
- **Immutable:** once built, it never changes. A change means building a **new image** with a new tag (`myapp:1.1`).
- Built in **layers**; unchanged layers are reused (cached).
entries.summary: An image is a read-only template for creating containers — like a class, while a container is an object.

entries.question: What is a Docker container?
entries.answer:
A container is a **running instance of an image**, with its own process, network and file system.

- **Created with:** `docker run myapp:1.0` (creates and starts it).
- **When it stops:** the process ends, but the container still exists and can be started again. Files written **inside** it are lost when the container is **removed** — keep important data in a volume or database.

```bash
docker ps          # running containers
docker stop app    # stop
docker rm app      # remove (its internal files are gone)
```
entries.summary: A container is a running instance of an image, with its own process, network and file system.

docker rm app      # remove (its internal files are gone)

entries.question: What is a Dockerfile?
entries.answer:
A text file with **step-by-step instructions to build an image**. It makes builds repeatable and lives in Git with the code.

```dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre      # base image
WORKDIR /app                     # working folder
COPY target/app.jar app.jar      # add the app
EXPOSE 8080                      # document the port
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]   # start command
```

Common instructions: `FROM`, `WORKDIR`, `COPY`, `RUN` (run a command at build time), `ENV`, `EXPOSE`, `CMD`/`ENTRYPOINT`.

entries.question: Why should applications inside Docker be stateless?
entries.answer:
Containers are **replaced all the time** (new version, crash, scaling). If a container stores data locally — uploaded files, sessions — that data **disappears** when it's replaced, and other copies of the app can't see it.

Keep state outside: database, Redis for sessions, S3 or a volume for files. Then any container can serve any request, and you can add or remove containers freely.
entries.summary: Containers are replaced all the time (new version, crash, scaling). If a container stores data locally — uploaded files, sessions — that data disappears when it's replaced, and other copies of the app can't see it.

entries.question: How do you pass configuration to a Docker container?
entries.answer:
Build **one image** and change its behaviour per environment from outside:

- **Environment variables** (most common):
  ```bash
  docker run -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod -e DB_URL=jdbc:postgresql://db/shop myapp:1.0
  ```
- **External config files** mounted as a volume: `-v ./config:/app/config`
- **Secrets** from a secret manager (or Docker/Kubernetes secrets) — never baked into the image.

- **Testing:** tests run against the same image and real services (Testcontainers) as production.
- **Deployment:** the exact tested image is deployed; rollback = run the previous tag.
- Also: better use of servers, easy scaling, and a standard unit for Kubernetes.

entries.question: What is Jenkins?
entries.answer: Jenkins is an open-source **automation server**. It watches your Git repository and automatically **builds, tests and deploys** your code on every change — the engine of CI/CD in many companies.
entries.summary: Jenkins is an open-source automation server. It watches your Git repository and automatically builds, tests and deploys your code on every change — the engine of CI/CD in many companies.

entries.question: What is CI/CD?
entries.answer:
- **Continuous Integration (CI):** every push is automatically **built and tested**, so problems are found within minutes, not at release time.
- **Continuous Delivery:** every change that passes is **ready to release**; a person clicks to deploy to production.
- **Continuous Deployment:** every passing change goes to **production automatically**, no manual step.

```text
push → build → unit tests → package → deploy to test → (approve) → deploy to prod
```

entries.question: Why do teams use Jenkins for CI/CD?
entries.answer:
It removes slow, error-prone manual work:

- No more "build on someone's laptop and copy the JAR".
- Broken code is caught right after the commit, with the author still in context.
- Every release follows the same steps, with logs of what was deployed and when.
- Huge plugin ecosystem (Git, Maven, Docker, Kubernetes, Slack…).

Alternatives: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Azure DevOps.

entries.question: What is a Jenkins pipeline?
entries.answer: A pipeline describes the **whole build-to-deploy process as code**, in stages. It is preferred over manual "freestyle" jobs because it is version-controlled, reviewable, repeatable, and shows each stage's status clearly.
entries.summary: A pipeline describes the whole build-to-deploy process as code, in stages. It is preferred over manual "freestyle" jobs because it is version-controlled, reviewable, repeatable, and shows each stage's status clearly.

entries.question: What is a Jenkinsfile?
entries.summary: The file that defines the pipeline, stored in the root of the repository next to the code. Stored in Git so pipeline changes are reviewed and versioned with the code, and every branch can have its own pipeline.

entries.question: Why is Jenkinsfile written in Groovy?
entries.answer: Jenkins itself runs on the **JVM**, and Groovy is a JVM scripting language — so pipelines can use Java libraries and Jenkins internals directly. Compared with plain YAML, Groovy allows **logic** (conditions, loops, functions); compared with Java, it's shorter and needs no compiling.
entries.summary: Jenkins itself runs on the JVM, and Groovy is a JVM scripting language — so pipelines can use Java libraries and Jenkins internals directly. Compared with plain YAML, Groovy allows logic (conditions, loops, functions); compared with Java, it's shorter and needs no compiling.

entries.question: What is Groovy?
entries.answer: Groovy is a scripting language **for the JVM**. It's very close to Java — most Java code is valid Groovy — but with shorter syntax (optional semicolons and types, closures, string interpolation). It's used in Jenkins pipelines, Gradle build scripts and Spock tests.
entries.summary: Groovy is a scripting language for the JVM. It's very close to Java — most Java code is valid Groovy — but with shorter syntax (optional semicolons and types, closures, string interpolation). It's used in Jenkins pipelines, Gradle build scripts and Spock tests.

entries.question: Is Groovy statically typed or dynamically typed?
entries.answer: **Dynamically typed by default** (`def x = 5`), with optional static typing (`@CompileStatic`). Dynamic typing suits pipelines because scripts are short and work with data whose shape varies (environment variables, JSON from tools), so less boilerplate is needed.
entries.summary: Dynamically typed by default (def x = 5), with optional static typing (@CompileStatic). Dynamic typing suits pipelines because scripts are short and work with data whose shape varies (environment variables, JSON from tools), so less boilerplate is needed.

entries.question: What are common stages in a Jenkins pipeline?
entries.answer:
| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| Checkout | Get the code from Git |
| Build | Compile (`mvn compile`, `npm run build`) |
| Test | Unit and integration tests, coverage |
| Code quality | SonarQube, lint, security scan |
| Package | JAR / Docker image, push to a registry |
| Deploy | To test, then (often with approval) to production |
entries.summary: Checkout: Get the code from Git; Build: Compile (mvn compile, npm run build); Test: Unit and integration tests, coverage; Code quality: SonarQube, lint, security scan; Package: JAR / Docker image, push to a registry; Deploy: To test, then (often with approval) to production

entries.question: How does Jenkins trigger a pipeline?
entries.answer:
- **Git commit / push** — a webhook from GitHub/GitLab tells Jenkins immediately (better than polling).
- **Pull request** — build and test the PR before merging.
- **Manual trigger** — a "Build Now" button, often with parameters.
- Also: a **schedule** (cron, e.g. nightly builds) or another job finishing.
entries.summary: Git commit / push — a webhook from GitHub/GitLab tells Jenkins immediately (better than polling). Pull request — build and test the PR before merging. Manual trigger — a "Build Now" button, often with parameters. Also: a schedule (cron, e.g. nightly builds) or another job finishing.

entries.question: What happens when a Jenkins build fails?
entries.answer: The pipeline **stops at the failing stage** (later stages like deploy don't run) and the build is marked red. Developers are notified by **email, Slack/Teams or a PR status check**, which can block merging. The fix is to read the console log, fix the code, and push again.
entries.summary: The pipeline stops at the failing stage (later stages like deploy don't run) and the build is marked red. Developers are notified by email, Slack/Teams or a PR status check, which can block merging. The fix is to read the console log, fix the code, and push again.
keywords: email, slack/teams or a pr status check

entries.question: What is the difference between Jenkins master and agent?
entries.answer:
- **Controller (master):** schedules jobs, stores configuration, shows the UI.
- **Agents:** separate machines/containers that **actually run the builds**.

Agents are needed so builds don't overload the controller, many builds can run in parallel, and builds can run in different environments (Linux, Windows, Java 17, Java 21).
entries.summary: Controller (master): schedules jobs, stores configuration, shows the UI. Agents: separate machines/containers that actually run the builds.

entries.question: Where is Groovy mostly used in Jenkins?
entries.answer:
- **Pipeline scripts** — the `Jenkinsfile`.
- **Shared libraries** — reusable Groovy functions (e.g. a standard `buildJavaService()` step) shared by many repositories, so each team's Jenkinsfile stays tiny.
- Also: admin scripts in the Jenkins script console.
entries.summary: Pipeline scripts — the Jenkinsfile. Shared libraries — reusable Groovy functions (e.g. a standard buildJavaService() step) shared by many repositories, so each team's Jenkinsfile stays tiny. Also: admin scripts in the Jenkins script console.

entries.question: What are common problems seen in Jenkins pipelines?
entries.answer:
| Problem | Typical fix |
|---|---|
| **Flaky builds** (pass/fail randomly) | Fix unstable tests; avoid shared state and timing waits |
| **Long execution time** | Cache dependencies, run stages in parallel, split slow tests |
| **Environment mismatch** ("works on agent A only") | Build inside Docker containers so every agent is identical |
| Secrets in logs | Use the Jenkins credentials store; mask values |
| Plugin upgrade breakage | Pin and test plugin versions |
entries.summary: Flaky builds (pass/fail randomly): Fix unstable tests; avoid shared state and timing waits; Long execution time: Cache dependencies, run stages in parallel, split slow tests; Environment mismatch ("works on agent A only"): Build inside Docker containers so every agent is identical; Secrets in logs: Use the Jenkins…

entries.question: What is Apache Tomcat?
entries.answer:
Tomcat is an open-source **web server and servlet container** for Java. It accepts HTTP requests and passes them to your Java code (servlets — Spring MVC is built on them).

It's a **web container**, not a full Java EE / Jakarta EE application server like WildFly or WebLogic (which add things like EJB and JMS).
entries.summary: Tomcat is an open-source web server and servlet container for Java. It accepts HTTP requests and passes them to your Java code (servlets — Spring MVC is built on them).

entries.question: What kind of applications run on Tomcat?
entries.answer: Java web applications and REST APIs built on **servlets**: Spring MVC / Spring Boot, JSP pages, plain servlet apps. It's common with Java because it's lightweight, free, stable, and the **default embedded server in Spring Boot**.
entries.summary: Java web applications and REST APIs built on servlets: Spring MVC / Spring Boot, JSP pages, plain servlet apps. It's common with Java because it's lightweight, free, stable, and the default embedded server in Spring Boot.
keywords: default embedded server in spring boot

entries.question: How does Tomcat handle incoming requests?
entries.answer:
**Thread-per-request:** a connector accepts the connection, then a thread from Tomcat's **thread pool** (200 threads by default) runs the request through filters and the servlet (Spring's `DispatcherServlet`) and writes the response. The thread then returns to the pool.

If all threads are busy (slow database calls), new requests wait in a queue — then time out. That's why slow downstream calls can "freeze" a Tomcat app. Java 21 **virtual threads** remove most of this limit.
entries.summary: Thread-per-request: a connector accepts the connection, then a thread from Tomcat's thread pool (200 threads by default) runs the request through filters and the servlet (Spring's DispatcherServlet) and writes the response. The thread then returns to the pool.

entries.question: What is a WAR file?
entries.answer:
A **Web Application Archive** — a ZIP of a Java web app (classes, libraries, `web.xml`, static files) made to run **inside an external server** like Tomcat.

Deploy it by copying it into Tomcat's `webapps/` folder (Tomcat unpacks and starts it) or via the Tomcat Manager.

Spring Boot apps are usually packaged as an executable **JAR** with Tomcat embedded instead.
entries.summary: A Web Application Archive — a ZIP of a Java web app (classes, libraries, web.xml, static files) made to run inside an external server like Tomcat.

entries.question: Difference between embedded Tomcat and external Tomcat?
entries.answer:
| Embedded Tomcat | External Tomcat |
|---|---|
| Tomcat is **inside your JAR** (`java -jar app.jar`) | You install Tomcat and **deploy WARs** into it |
| One app per process; config in `application.yml` | Several apps can share one server |
| Perfect for Docker and microservices | Traditional/legacy setups |

Spring Boot uses embedded Tomcat because the app becomes **self-contained** — no server to install or configure separately, and the same JAR runs everywhere.
entries.summary: Spring Boot uses embedded Tomcat because the app becomes self-contained — no server to install or configure separately, and the same JAR runs everywhere.

entries.question: What are common issues seen in Tomcat?
entries.answer:
- **Port conflicts** — "Address already in use: 8080" → stop the other process or change `server.port`.
- **Memory issues** — `OutOfMemoryError` from leaks or too small a heap → heap dumps, `-Xmx`, fix leaks.
- **Thread exhaustion** — all request threads stuck on slow calls → timeouts, more threads, async or virtual threads.
- Also: class-loading conflicts between WAR libraries, and memory leaks on repeated redeploys.
entries.summary: Port conflicts — "Address already in use: 8080" → stop the other process or change server.port. Memory issues — OutOfMemoryError from leaks or too small a heap → heap dumps, -Xmx, fix leaks. Thread exhaustion — all request threads stuck on slow calls → timeouts, more threads, async or virtual threads. Also:…

entries.question: How do you restart or redeploy applications in Tomcat?
entries.answer:
- **Manual:** `shutdown.sh` / `startup.sh`, or replace the WAR in `webapps/` (Tomcat redeploys it), or use the Tomcat Manager UI.
- **Automated (better):** the CI/CD pipeline deploys the new version; with containers, you deploy a new image and the orchestrator (Kubernetes) replaces old containers with a **rolling update** — no manual restarts.
entries.summary: Manual: shutdown.sh / startup.sh, or replace the WAR in webapps/ (Tomcat redeploys it), or use the Tomcat Manager UI. Automated (better): the CI/CD pipeline deploys the new version; with containers, you deploy a new image and the orchestrator (Kubernetes) replaces old containers with a rolling update — no manual…

entries.question: What is Maven and why is it used?
entries.answer:
Maven is a **build and dependency management tool** for Java. It solves:

- **Dependencies:** you list libraries; Maven downloads them (and their dependencies).
- **Standard build:** the same commands (`mvn package`) and folder layout (`src/main/java`) in every project.
- **Repeatable builds** on any machine and in CI.
entries.summary: Maven is a build and dependency management tool for Java. It solves:

entries.question: What is a `pom.xml` file?
entries.answer:
The **Project Object Model** — Maven's configuration file. It contains the project's identity (`groupId`, `artifactId`, `version`), packaging (JAR/WAR), Java version, **dependencies**, plugins and build settings.

```xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>
```
entries.summary: The Project Object Model — Maven's configuration file. It contains the project's identity (groupId, artifactId, version), packaging (JAR/WAR), Java version, dependencies, plugins and build settings.

  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
</dependency>

entries.question: What is dependency management in Maven?
entries.answer:
You declare **what** you need; Maven fetches it, plus everything **it** needs (**transitive dependencies**), and puts them on the classpath. How it downloads: checks the local repository (`~/.m2`) → if missing, downloads from **Maven Central** (or your company's repository) → caches it locally. ```mermaid flowchart LR P["pom.xml: needs spring-web"] --> L{"In ~/.m2 local repo?"} L -- yes --> CP[Put on classpath] L -- no --> R["Download from Maven Central
or company Nexus"] R --> S[Save in ~/.m2] --> CP P -. "also pulls its dependencies
(transitive)" .-> T["spring-core, jackson, ..."] ``` - **Scopes:** `compile` (default), `test` (only for tests), `provided` (server supplies it), `runtime`. - **Version conflicts:** the "nearest" declaration wins; inspect with `mvn dependency:tree`, fix with `` or ``.
entries.summary: You declare what you need; Maven fetches it, plus everything it needs (transitive dependencies), and puts them on the classpath.

or company Nexus"] R --> S[Save in ~/.m2] --> CP P -. "also pulls its dependencies
(transitive)" .-> T["spring-core, jackson, ..."]

entries.question: What are Maven repositories?
entries.answer:
- **Local** — `~/.m2/repository` on your machine; a cache of everything downloaded.
- **Central** — the public Maven Central repository.
- **Remote** — any other server, usually a company repository (Nexus, Artifactory) that stores internal libraries and caches Central.

Lookup order: local → remote/central.
entries.summary: Local — ~/.m2/repository on your machine; a cache of everything downloaded. Central — the public Maven Central repository. Remote — any other server, usually a company repository (Nexus, Artifactory) that stores internal libraries and caches Central.

entries.question: What is the Maven build lifecycle?
entries.answer:
An ordered list of **phases**. Running a phase runs **all phases before it**.

| Phase | Does |
|---|---|
| `validate` | Checks the project is correct |
| `compile` | Compiles main code |
| `test` | Runs unit tests |
| `package` | Builds the JAR/WAR in `target/` |
| `verify` | Runs integration checks |
| `install` | Copies the artifact to your **local** repository |
| `deploy` | Uploads it to a **remote** repository |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  V[validate] --> C[compile] --> T[test] --> P[package] --> VE[verify] --> I[install] --> D[deploy]
  style P fill:#d4efdf
```

`mvn clean package` = delete `target/`, then validate → compile → test → package.
entries.summary: An ordered list of phases. Running a phase runs all phases before it.

  style P fill:#d4efdf

entries.question: What is a Maven plugin?
entries.answer: Plugins do the **actual work** of each phase — Maven itself is mostly a framework that runs them. Examples: `maven-compiler-plugin` (compile), `maven-surefire-plugin` (unit tests), `maven-failsafe-plugin` (integration tests), `spring-boot-maven-plugin` (executable JAR), `jacoco-maven-plugin` (coverage).
entries.summary: Plugins do the actual work of each phase — Maven itself is mostly a framework that runs them. Examples: maven-compiler-plugin (compile), maven-surefire-plugin (unit tests), maven-failsafe-plugin (integration tests), spring-boot-maven-plugin (executable JAR), jacoco-maven-plugin (coverage).

entries.question: What is a multi-module Maven project?
entries.answer:
One **parent project with several modules** (sub-projects), built together with one command.

```text
shop-parent/
├── pom.xml          (parent: shared versions and plugins)
├── shop-common/     (shared DTOs, utilities)
├── shop-api/        (REST app, depends on common)
└── shop-batch/      (batch jobs, depends on common)
```

Teams use it to share code and dependency versions, keep clear module boundaries, and build everything in the right order.
entries.summary: One parent project with several modules (sub-projects), built together with one command.

entries.question: How does Maven help maintain consistency across environments?
entries.answer: **Same build everywhere:** the `pom.xml` pins dependency and plugin versions, and Maven uses the same lifecycle on every laptop and CI agent. The **Maven Wrapper** (`./mvnw`) even pins the Maven version itself. Result: the JAR built in CI is the same one that was tested.
entries.summary: Same build everywhere: the pom.xml pins dependency and plugin versions, and Maven uses the same lifecycle on every laptop and CI agent. The Maven Wrapper (./mvnw) even pins the Maven version itself. Result: the JAR built in CI is the same one that was tested.

entries.question: Typical CI/CD flow using these tools?
entries.answer:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Code commit] --> B[Jenkins pipeline starts]
  B --> C[Maven build + tests]
  C --> D[Docker image built and pushed]
  D --> E[Deploy to test]
  E --> F[Deploy to production]
```

1. Developer pushes code → webhook starts Jenkins.
2. **Maven** compiles, tests and packages the JAR.
3. **Docker** builds an image with the JAR and pushes it to a registry.
4. The image is deployed (Docker host or Kubernetes); the Spring Boot app runs with **embedded Tomcat** inside.
entries.summary: Developer pushes code → webhook starts Jenkins. Maven compiles, tests and packages the JAR. Docker builds an image with the JAR and pushes it to a registry. The image is deployed (Docker host or Kubernetes); the Spring Boot app runs with embedded Tomcat inside.

entries.question: How do Maven, Jenkins, and Docker work together?
entries.answer:
Each tool has one responsibility:

- **Jenkins** — the **orchestrator**: decides when to run and runs each step.
- **Maven** — **builds** the Java code into a tested JAR.
- **Docker** — **packages** the JAR with its runtime into an image that runs anywhere.
entries.summary: Each tool has one responsibility:

entries.question: Where does Tomcat fit in this flow?
entries.answer: At **runtime**. In modern Spring Boot apps, Tomcat is **embedded in the JAR**, which runs **inside the Docker container** — no separate Tomcat installation. In older setups, Maven builds a WAR that is deployed to a standalone Tomcat server.
entries.summary: At runtime. In modern Spring Boot apps, Tomcat is embedded in the JAR, which runs inside the Docker container — no separate Tomcat installation. In older setups, Maven builds a WAR that is deployed to a standalone Tomcat server.

entries.question: What problems do these tools solve together?
entries.answer:
| Problem | Solved by |
|---|---|
| **Environment inconsistency** ("works on my machine") | Docker images + Maven-pinned versions |
| **Manual deployments** (slow, risky, undocumented) | Jenkins pipelines |
| **Build failures found late** | CI builds and tests every commit |
| Hard rollbacks | Versioned Docker images — redeploy the previous tag |
entries.summary: Environment inconsistency ("works on my machine"): Docker images + Maven-pinned versions; Manual deployments (slow, risky, undocumented): Jenkins pipelines; Build failures found late: CI builds and tests every commit; Hard rollbacks: Versioned Docker images — redeploy the previous tag

entries.question: How do you approach a system design interview?
entries.answer:
Follow the same five steps every time, and talk out loud while you do it.

1. **Clarify requirements** — what must it do (features), and how well (users, speed, availability)?
2. **Estimate scale** — users per day, requests per second, data per year.
3. **Draw the high-level design** — client → load balancer → services → database / cache / queue.
4. **Go deep on 1–2 parts** — the database schema, the hardest API, or the bottleneck.
5. **Discuss trade-offs** — what fails, how it scales, what you would do next.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Requirements] --> B[Estimates] --> C[High-level design] --> D[Deep dive] --> E[Trade-offs]
```

> 💡 **Tip:** Interviewers score how you think, not one "right" diagram. Ask questions before drawing.
entries.summary: Follow the same five steps every time, and talk out loud while you do it.

  A[Requirements] --> B[Estimates] --> C[High-level design] --> D[Deep dive] --> E[Trade-offs]

entries.question: What is the difference between functional and non-functional requirements?
entries.answer: ↪ Functional = what the system does ("users can post a photo"). Non-functional = how well it does it ("loads in under 200 ms, 99.9% uptime").
entries.summary: Functional = what the system does ("users can post a photo"). Non-functional = how well it does it ("loads in under 200 ms, 99.9% uptime").

entries.question: How long should each step take in a 45-minute interview?
entries.answer: ↪ About 5 min requirements, 5 min estimates, 10–15 min high-level design, 15 min deep dive, 5 min trade-offs.
entries.summary: About 5 min requirements, 5 min estimates, 10–15 min high-level design, 15 min deep dive, 5 min trade-offs.

entries.question: How do you do back-of-the-envelope estimation?
entries.answer:
Round everything to simple numbers and multiply. The goal is the **order of magnitude**, not an exact answer.

**Handy numbers**

| Fact | Value |
|---|---|
| Seconds in a day | ~100,000 (86,400) |
| 1 million requests/day | ~12 requests/second |
| 1 KB × 1 million | 1 GB |
| Peak traffic | ~2–3× average |

**Example — a photo app with 10 million daily users, each uploading 2 photos of 500 KB:**

- Uploads: 20 M/day ÷ 100,000 s ≈ **200 uploads/s** (peak ~500/s)
- Storage: 20 M × 500 KB = **10 TB per day** → ~3.6 PB per year → needs object storage (like S3), not a database
entries.summary: Round everything to simple numbers and multiply. The goal is the order of magnitude, not an exact answer.

entries.question: Why do estimates matter?
entries.answer: ↪ They decide the design: 10 requests/s fits one server and one database; 100,000 requests/s needs caching, sharding and many servers.
entries.summary: They decide the design: 10 requests/s fits one server and one database; 100,000 requests/s needs caching, sharding and many servers.

entries.question: What is the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling?
entries.answer:
- **Vertical scaling (scale up)** — make one machine bigger (more CPU, RAM). Simple, but there is a maximum size and it is a single point of failure.
- **Horizontal scaling (scale out)** — add more machines and split the work. No real limit, survives a machine failing, but needs a load balancer and stateless services.

```text
Vertical:   [ small server ]  →  [ BIG server ]
Horizontal: [ server ]        →  [ server ][ server ][ server ]  (behind a load balancer)
```
entries.summary: Vertical scaling (scale up) — make one machine bigger (more CPU, RAM). Simple, but there is a maximum size and it is a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling (scale out) — add more machines and split the work. No real limit, survives a machine failing, but needs a load balancer and stateless services.

codeBlocks.code:

Horizontal: [ server ]        →  [ server ][ server ][ server ]  (behind a load balancer)

entries.question: Why must services be stateless to scale horizontally?
entries.answer: ↪ Any server may get the next request. If the session lives in one server's memory, other servers don't know the user. Keep state in a shared store (Redis, database) or in a token (JWT).
entries.summary: Any server may get the next request. If the session lives in one server's memory, other servers don't know the user. Keep state in a shared store (Redis, database) or in a token (JWT).

entries.question: What is a load balancer and how does it decide where to send a request?
entries.answer:
A load balancer sits in front of several servers and spreads incoming requests across them, so no single server is overloaded. It also stops sending traffic to servers that fail health checks.

**Common algorithms**

| Algorithm | How it picks | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| Round robin | Next server in turn | Servers of equal size |
| Least connections | Server with fewest active requests | Requests of different lengths |
| IP hash | Same client → same server | Simple "sticky" sessions |
| Weighted | Bigger servers get more | Mixed server sizes |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  U[Users] --> LB[Load balancer]
  LB --> S1[Server 1]
  LB --> S2[Server 2]
  LB --> S3[Server 3]
```
entries.summary: A load balancer sits in front of several servers and spreads incoming requests across them, so no single server is overloaded. It also stops sending traffic to servers that fail health checks.

flowchart LR
  U[Users] --> LB[Load balancer]
  LB --> S1[Server 1]
  LB --> S2[Server 2]
