entries.question: How do CPU registers, L1/L2/L3 cache, RAM and disk interact?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?** A **memory hierarchy**: small and fast near the CPU, big and slow further away. Data moves up the hierarchy when it is used. | Level | Typical size | Typical latency | |---|---|---| | Registers | ~16 general-purpose (x86-64) | ~0.3 ns | | L1 cache (per core) | 32–64 KB | ~1 ns | | L2 cache (per core) | 256 KB–2 MB | ~3–5 ns | | L3 cache (shared) | 8–64 MB | ~10–20 ns | | RAM | 8–128 GB | ~80–100 ns | | SSD | TBs | ~50–100 µs | **2. How does it work internally?** 1. An instruction needs data at an address. 2. Check **L1** → miss → **L2** → miss → **L3** → miss → **RAM**. 3. The data comes back as a whole **64-byte cache line** and is stored in each level on the way. 4. If the page isn't in RAM at all, a **page fault** makes the OS read it from disk. **3. Visual** ```mermaid flowchart LR REG[Registers] <--> L1["L1
per core"] <--> L2["L2
per core"] <--> L3["L3
shared"] <--> RAM[(RAM)] <-. "page fault /
swap" .-> DISK[(SSD / disk)] ``` **4. Internal implementation** - Caches are **set-associative**: an address maps to a small set of slots; the oldest line in the set is evicted (approximate LRU). - **Write-back**: writes go to the cache and reach RAM later, when the line is evicted. - **Cache coherence (MESI protocol)**: when one core writes a line, other cores' copies are invalidated, so all cores see the same value. - **Prefetchers** detect sequential access and fetch the next lines early. **5. Why is it designed this way?** Fast memory is expensive and must be physically close to the core. Most programs reuse recent data (**temporal locality**) and nearby data (**spatial locality**), so small caches catch most accesses (often 95%+ hit rate). **6. Language differences** Languages that lay data out **contiguously** (C/C++/Rust/Go structs and arrays, Java `int[]`) use caches well. A Java `ArrayList` or Python list holds **pointers** to objects scattered on the heap → more cache misses. **7. Practical example** ```java int[][] m = new int[4096][4096]; for (int i...) for (int j...) sum += m[i][j]; // row by row: fast (sequential) for (int j...) for (int i...) sum += m[i][j]; // column by column: often 5-10x slower (cache misses) ``` **8. How can I observe it?** - `perf stat -e cache-references,cache-misses ./app` (Linux); Intel VTune memory analysis. - `lscpu` (Linux) or Task Manager → Performance → CPU shows your L1/L2/L3 sizes.

entries.question: What exactly is stored in Stack and Heap memory?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?** Two regions of a program's memory: - **Stack** — one per thread. Holds **call frames**: local variables, parameters, return addresses. Freed automatically when a function returns. - **Heap** — shared by all threads. Holds data whose size or lifetime isn't tied to one function call (objects, arrays, strings). **2. How does it work internally?** 1. Calling a function pushes a **frame**: the **stack pointer** register just moves down by the frame size. 2. Locals live in that frame (or in registers). 3. `new` / `malloc` asks the heap allocator for a block and returns its **address**. 4. Returning pops the frame (stack pointer moves back). Heap blocks stay until freed (manually, by ownership rules or by GC). **3. Visual** ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Stack["Stack (thread 1)"] F2["frame: createUser()
name = ref → heap
age = 30"] F1["frame: main()
user = ref → heap"] end subgraph Heap U["User object
{name, age}"] S["String Asha"] end F1 -- reference --> U U --> S F2 -- reference --> S ``` **4. Internal implementation** - Stack allocation = one pointer subtraction: extremely fast, no fragmentation. Size is fixed per thread (e.g. 512 KB–1 MB default for Java threads; `-Xss`). Too deep recursion → **StackOverflowError**. - Heap allocation needs an allocator (free lists, size classes) or a GC with bump-pointer allocation. - **Java**: primitives and references in frames live on the stack; all objects on the heap. The JIT's **escape analysis** can avoid heap allocation for objects that never leave a method. **5. Why is it designed this way?** Most data is short-lived and tied to a call → the stack handles it for free. Data that must outlive a call or be shared needs the heap, which is flexible but costs allocation time and cleanup. **6. Language differences** | Language | Stack | Heap | |---|---|---| | C / C++ | Locals, structs, arrays by value | `malloc` / `new`; you free it | | Rust | Values by default | `Box`, `Vec`, `String`; freed by ownership | | Go | Compiler decides by **escape analysis** | Escaping values; GC frees | | Java | Primitives + references | All objects; GC frees | | C# | Locals, value types (`struct`) | Class instances; GC frees | | Python / JS | Interpreter's own frames | Essentially every value is a heap object | **7. Practical example** ```java int total(int[] prices) { // 'prices' (a reference) is in this frame int sum = 0; // 'sum' in this frame (or a register) for (int p : prices) sum += p; return sum; // frame popped; the array stays on the heap while referenced } ``` **8. How can I observe it?** - Java: IntelliJ debugger "Frames" (stack) and "Variables"; VisualVM heap dump (heap). - Chrome DevTools: Sources → Call Stack panel; Memory → heap snapshot. - Go: `go build -gcflags=-m` prints which variables "escape to heap".

entries.question: Can the CPU directly access heap memory? How does a program access objects in RAM?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?** **Yes.** The heap is ordinary memory; the CPU reads it with normal load/store instructions. But every address a program uses is a **virtual address** that hardware translates to a physical RAM address. **2. How does it work internally?** 1. Your variable holds a **reference/pointer** = a virtual address (e.g. `0x7f3a1c00`). 2. Reading `user.age` becomes: load from `address + offset of age`. 3. The **MMU** (Memory Management Unit) translates virtual → physical, first checking the **TLB** (a cache of recent translations). 4. TLB miss → the hardware walks the **page tables** (4 levels on x86-64). 5. With the physical address, the data comes from L1/L2/L3 or RAM. **3. Visual** ```mermaid flowchart LR I["mov eax, [rbx+12]
read user.age"] --> VA["Virtual address
0x7f3a1c0c"] VA --> TLB{"TLB hit?"} TLB -- yes --> PA[Physical address] TLB -- no --> PW["Page-table walk
4 levels"] --> PA PA --> C{"In L1/L2/L3?"} C -- yes --> R[Value in register] C -- no --> RAM[(RAM)] --> R ``` **4. Internal implementation** - An object is a block of bytes; each field sits at a **fixed offset** decided by the compiler/runtime (Java object header ~12–16 bytes, then fields). - Java uses **compressed oops**: 32-bit references scaled ×8, so heaps up to ~32 GB use half the memory per reference. - Moving GCs relocate objects and **update every reference** to them, so references stay valid. **5. Why is it designed this way?** Virtual addresses give each process a private, protected address space and let the OS place pages anywhere in RAM (or on disk). The TLB keeps translation cheap for the common case. **6. Language differences** - **C/C++** — raw pointers; pointer arithmetic allowed; invalid pointers → crashes or security bugs. - **Rust** — references checked at compile time; raw pointers only in `unsafe`. - **Java / C# / Go / JS / Python** — references you can't do arithmetic on; runtime prevents invalid access (`NullPointerException` instead of reading random memory). **7. Practical example** ```java User u = new User("Asha", 30); // u = reference (address) to a heap object int a = u.age; // JIT emits: load [u + offset_of_age] ``` **8. How can I observe it?** - Java: **JOL** (Java Object Layout) prints field offsets and object sizes: `ClassLayout.parseClass(User.class).toPrintable()`. - C: `printf("%p", &x)` prints virtual addresses; run twice — ASLR changes them. - Linux `perf stat -e dTLB-load-misses ./app`.

entries.question: How does memory allocation and deallocation work?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?** **Allocation** = finding a free block of memory big enough for new data. **Deallocation** = returning it so it can be reused. Done by an **allocator** (C/C++/Rust) or a **managed runtime** (Java, C#, Go, JS, Python). **2. How does it work internally?** 1. The program asks for N bytes (`malloc(64)`, `new User()`). 2. The allocator looks in its **free lists** / **size classes** for a fitting block. 3. If none, it asks the OS for more memory (`mmap`/`brk` on Linux, `VirtualAlloc` on Windows), in big chunks. 4. It returns the block's address. 5. On free (or when GC finds it dead), the block goes back to a free list (or the region is reclaimed in bulk). **3. Visual** ```mermaid flowchart TD A["new / malloc(64)"] --> B{"Free block of
this size class?"} B -- yes --> C[Return its address] B -- no --> D["Ask OS for more pages
mmap / VirtualAlloc"] --> E[Split into blocks] --> C F["free() / GC finds it dead"] --> G[Block back to free list] G -.-> B ``` **4. Internal implementation** - **malloc** (glibc ptmalloc, jemalloc, tcmalloc, mimalloc): size classes, per-thread caches to avoid locks, large blocks straight from `mmap`. - **JVM**: each thread gets a **TLAB** (Thread-Local Allocation Buffer); allocating is a **bump pointer** — add the size to a pointer. Almost as fast as stack allocation. - **Fragmentation**: free memory split into small holes. Compacting GCs (Java, .NET, V8) move live objects together to fix it; `malloc` can't move blocks. **5. Why is it designed this way?** Asking the OS for every allocation would be very slow (system calls), so allocators grab large chunks and manage them in user space. Bump-pointer + compacting GC makes allocation cheap, at the cost of GC work later. **6. Language differences** | Language | Allocate | Free | |---|---|---| | C | `malloc` | `free` (manual) | | C++ | `new`, `make_unique` | `delete` or destructor (RAII) | | Rust | `Box::new`, `Vec` | Automatic `drop` when owner goes out of scope | | Java / C# | `new` (TLAB bump pointer) | Tracing GC | | Go | Compiler escape analysis + size-class allocator | Concurrent GC | | Python | `pymalloc` for small objects | Reference count hits 0 (+ cycle GC) | **7. Practical example** ```c char *buf = malloc(1024); // allocator returns a block address strcpy(buf, "hi"); free(buf); // block returns to the free list // using buf now = "use after free" bug ``` **8. How can I observe it?** - C/C++: **Valgrind** or AddressSanitizer (`-fsanitize=address`) find leaks and use-after-free. - Java: VisualVM / JFR "Allocation" view; `-Xlog:gc` shows heap before/after each GC. - Windows: Process Explorer → Private Bytes growing steadily = possible leak.
entries.summary: What is it? Allocation = finding a free block of memory big enough for new data. Deallocation = returning it so it can be reused. Done by an allocator (C/C++/Rust) or a managed runtime (Java, C#, Go, JS, Python).

entries.question: How does Garbage Collection identify unused objects?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?**
A **garbage collector** frees heap objects the program can no longer use, so you don't call `free`. "Unused" means **unreachable**: no chain of references leads to it from the running program.

**2. How does it work internally?**
Tracing GC (Java, C#, Go, JavaScript):

1. Start from **GC roots**: local variables in thread stacks, static fields, CPU registers, JNI handles.
2. **Mark** every object reachable by following references.
3. Everything not marked is garbage → **sweep** (add to free list) or **compact/copy** live objects together.

Reference counting (CPython): each object counts references to it; at 0 it is freed immediately; a separate cycle detector handles A↔B loops.

**3. Visual**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  R1["Root: local var 'order'"] --> O[Order]
  R2["Root: static cache"] --> C[Customer]
  O --> I[Item list]
  O --> C
  X1[Old Cart] --> X2[Old Item]
  X2 --> X1
  style X1 fill:#fde2e1
  style X2 fill:#fde2e1
```

Red objects reference each other but nothing reachable points to them → garbage (a tracing GC frees cycles).

**4. Internal implementation**

- **Tri-colour marking**: white (not seen), grey (seen, children not scanned), black (done). Lets marking run **concurrently** with the program.
- **Write barriers**: small code the JIT adds to every reference write, so the GC notices changes made while it marks.
- **Generational GC**: most objects die young, so the **young generation** is collected often by copying survivors; **card tables** track old→young references so the GC doesn't scan the whole old generation.

**5. Why is it designed this way?**
Reachability is safe: an unreachable object can never be used again. Generations make collection cheap because young garbage is cheap to discard. Costs: CPU time, extra memory headroom, and pauses (modern collectors like ZGC keep them to around a millisecond).

**6. Language differences**

| Runtime | Method |
|---|---|
| Java (HotSpot) | Generational tracing: G1 default; ZGC, Shenandoah for low pause |
| C# (.NET) | Generational tracing (gen 0/1/2 + large object heap) |
| Go | Concurrent mark-sweep, **non-generational**, non-moving |
| JavaScript (V8) | Generational: young gen copying (Scavenger), old gen mark-compact (Orinoco) |
| Python (CPython) | Reference counting + generational cycle collector |
| Rust / C / C++ | No GC (ownership / manual / RAII) |

**7. Practical example**

```java
List<byte[]> cache = new ArrayList<>();   // static field → a GC root
void handle() {
    byte[] tmp = new byte[1024];          // unreachable after return → collected
    cache.add(new byte[1024]);            // reachable from the root forever → "memory leak" in Java
}
```

**8. How can I observe it?**

- Java: `-Xlog:gc*` or VisualVM "Monitor" tab (heap sawtooth = normal GC); heap dump → Eclipse MAT "dominator tree" finds what keeps objects alive.
- Chrome DevTools → Memory → compare two heap snapshots to find leaks.
- Python: `import gc; gc.get_count()`; `sys.getrefcount(obj)`.

entries.question: How do Processes and Threads work internally?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?** - **Process** — a running program with its **own** virtual address space, open files and resources. Isolated from other processes. - **Thread** — a path of execution **inside** a process. Threads share the process's memory (heap, code) but each has its **own stack and registers**. **2. How does it work internally?** 1. Starting a program: the OS creates a process (`fork`+`exec` on Linux, `CreateProcess` on Windows), sets up its page tables, loads the code, and starts the **main thread**. 2. Creating a thread (`pthread_create`, `new Thread().start()`): the OS allocates a stack and a **thread control block** (saved registers, state, priority). 3. The **scheduler** picks which threads run on which CPU cores. **3. Visual** ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph P1["Process A (own address space)"] H1[(Heap + code + globals)] T1["Thread 1
stack + registers"] --> H1 T2["Thread 2
stack + registers"] --> H1 end subgraph P2["Process B (separate address space)"] H2[(Heap + code + globals)] T3["Thread 1"] --> H2 end K["OS kernel: scheduler,
page tables, process/thread tables"] --> P1 K --> P2 ``` **4. Internal implementation** - Linux represents both as `task_struct`; threads are tasks that share the same memory map (`clone` with `CLONE_VM`). - Each process has its own **page tables** → address `0x1000` in A and in B are different physical memory. - Threads talk through shared memory (needs locks); processes talk through **IPC**: pipes, sockets, shared memory segments. **5. Why is it designed this way?** Processes give **isolation** (a crash or bug in one can't corrupt another). Threads give **cheap concurrency** within one program (shared data, no copying). Trade-off: shared memory → race conditions; processes → heavier and slower to communicate. **6. Language differences** | Language | Concurrency unit | Maps to | |---|---|---| | Java | `Thread` (platform); **virtual threads** (Java 21) | 1 OS thread; many virtual threads on few OS threads | | C# | Threads + `async/await` tasks on a thread pool | OS threads | | Go | **Goroutines** | Many goroutines on few OS threads (M:N scheduler) | | JavaScript | One main thread + event loop; Web Workers / worker_threads | Each worker = separate thread + isolate | | Python | Threads, but the **GIL** lets one run Python code at a time (optional free-threaded build since 3.13); `multiprocessing` for CPU work | OS threads / processes | | Rust / C++ | `std::thread` | OS threads | **7. Practical example** A Spring Boot app is **one process** (the JVM) with many threads: Tomcat request threads (`http-nio-8080-exec-1…`), GC threads, JIT compiler threads. **8. How can I observe it?** - Windows **Process Explorer**: a process → Properties → Threads tab. - Java: `jcmd Thread.print` or VisualVM → Threads. - Linux: `ps -eLf` (threads), `top -H -p `.
entries.summary: Process — a running program with its own virtual address space, open files and resources. Isolated from other processes. Thread — a path of execution inside a process. Threads share the process's memory (heap, code) but each has its own stack and registers.

entries.question: How does Context Switching happen?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?**
A **context switch** is the OS pausing one thread on a CPU core and resuming another. The "context" is everything needed to continue later: registers, instruction pointer, stack pointer.

**2. How does it work internally?**

1. Trigger: a **timer interrupt** (time slice used up), the thread **blocks** (waiting for I/O or a lock), or a higher-priority thread becomes ready.
2. The CPU jumps into the kernel and saves the current thread's registers into its kernel data.
3. The **scheduler** picks the next thread to run.
4. If it belongs to a **different process**, the CPU switches page tables (CR3 register on x86).
5. The new thread's registers are restored and it continues exactly where it stopped.

**3. Visual**

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant A as Thread A
  participant K as Kernel scheduler
  participant B as Thread B
  A->>K: Timer interrupt / blocks on I/O
  K->>K: Save A's registers, IP, SP
  K->>K: Pick next thread (B)
  K->>K: Switch page tables if B is another process
  K->>B: Restore B's registers, jump to its IP
  Note over A: A waits until scheduled again
```

**4. Internal implementation**

- Linux scheduler: **CFS** (Completely Fair Scheduler) for years, replaced by **EEVDF** in kernel 6.6; it picks the thread that has had the least fair share of CPU.
- Direct cost: ~1–5 µs. Hidden cost: the new thread finds cold **caches and TLB** (PCID on x86 avoids a full TLB flush).
- Switching between threads of the **same** process is cheaper (no page-table switch).

**5. Why is it designed this way?**
Preemption (forced switching) means one busy or stuck thread can't freeze the whole machine. The cost is overhead — which is why thousands of OS threads perform badly, and why runtimes added lightweight threads.

**6. Language differences**
User-space scheduling avoids kernel switches: **Go goroutines**, **Java virtual threads**, **Kotlin coroutines**, **C#/JS/Python async** switch tasks inside the runtime when they wait, which is much cheaper than an OS context switch.

**7. Practical example**
A Tomcat thread calls a slow database. While it waits on the socket, the OS switches that core to another request thread. With Java 21 virtual threads, the JVM instead **unmounts** the virtual thread and runs another one on the same OS thread — no OS context switch.

**8. How can I observe it?**

- Linux: `vmstat 1` (column `cs` = context switches/second), `pidstat -w`.
- Windows: Performance Monitor → "Context Switches/sec"; Process Explorer → thread "Context Switch Delta".
entries.summary: What is it? A context switch is the OS pausing one thread on a CPU core and resuming another. The "context" is everything needed to continue later: registers, instruction pointer, stack pointer.

entries.question: How does an operating system execute multiple applications simultaneously?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?**
Two mechanisms combined:

- **Parallelism** — different threads run **at the same instant** on different CPU cores.
- **Time-sharing (concurrency)** — each core switches between threads every few milliseconds, so it *looks* simultaneous.

**2. How does it work internally?**

1. Every thread is either **running**, **ready** (waiting for a core) or **blocked** (waiting for I/O, a lock, a timer).
2. The scheduler keeps **run queues** of ready threads per core.
3. Each core runs a thread until its time slice ends, it blocks, or something more important arrives.
4. Blocked threads use no CPU; when their I/O completes, an interrupt moves them back to ready.

**3. Visual**

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Ready
  Ready --> Running: scheduler picks it
  Running --> Ready: time slice ends
  Running --> Blocked: waits for disk / network / lock
  Blocked --> Ready: I/O done (interrupt)
  Running --> [*]: exits
```

**4. Internal implementation**

- Per-core run queues + **load balancing** that moves threads between cores.
- **Priorities** and fairness (Linux EEVDF, Windows priority-based preemptive scheduler with boosts for the foreground window).
- **DMA** (Direct Memory Access): disks and network cards copy data into RAM without the CPU, then raise an interrupt.

**5. Why is it designed this way?**
Most programs spend most time **waiting** (user input, disk, network). Giving the CPU to someone else while waiting keeps cores busy and the UI responsive.

**6. Language differences**
At OS level every language's threads are scheduled the same way. The difference is **how many OS threads** a program uses: Node.js uses one main thread plus a small pool; Java/C# traditionally one thread per request; Go multiplexes goroutines onto ~one OS thread per core.

**7. Practical example**
An 8-core laptop running Chrome, IntelliJ and Spotify may have **3,000+ threads**, but at most 8 (or 16 with hyper-threading) run at any instant; the rest are ready or, mostly, blocked.

**8. How can I observe it?**

- Windows Task Manager → Performance → CPU: "Processes", "Threads" counts and per-core graphs.
- Linux `htop`: per-core usage; `uptime` load average = average number of running + ready threads.

entries.question: How do Virtual Memory, Paging and Memory Protection work?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?**

- **Virtual memory** — each process sees its own private address space, as if it had all memory to itself.
- **Paging** — that space is split into fixed-size **pages** (usually 4 KB) mapped to physical **frames** in RAM, or not loaded at all.
- **Memory protection** — each page has permissions (read/write/execute, user/kernel), enforced by hardware.

**2. How does it work internally?**

1. The OS builds **page tables** for each process: virtual page → physical frame + permission bits.
2. On every access, the MMU translates the address (cached in the TLB).
3. Page **not present** → **page fault** → the OS loads it (from the executable, a file, or swap), updates the table, retries the instruction.
4. Permission violated (write to read-only, execute data, user touching kernel memory) → the OS kills the access: **segmentation fault** / **access violation**.

**3. Visual**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph PA["Process A virtual pages"]
    A0[page 0: code]
    A1[page 1: heap]
  end
  subgraph PB["Process B virtual pages"]
    B0[page 0: code]
    B1[page 1: heap]
  end
  subgraph RAM["Physical RAM frames"]
    F7[frame 7]
    F2[frame 2]
    F9[frame 9]
  end
  SW[(Swap / page file)]
  A0 -- "R-X" --> F7
  B0 -- "R-X shared library" --> F7
  A1 -- "RW-" --> F2
  B1 -- "RW-" --> F9
  B1 -. "if evicted" .-> SW
```

**4. Internal implementation**

- x86-64 uses **4-level page tables** (5-level on newer CPUs), each level indexed by 9 bits of the address.
- Permission bits: Present, Read/Write, User/Supervisor, **NX** (no-execute — stops running code injected into data).
- **Copy-on-write**: after `fork`, parent and child share pages until one writes.
- **ASLR**: code, stack and heap are placed at random addresses to make exploits harder.

**5. Why is it designed this way?**
Isolation (one program can't read another's memory), simple programming (every process starts from the same layout), sharing (one copy of a library in RAM for all processes), and the ability to use more memory than RAM via swap — though heavy swapping makes everything very slow ("thrashing").

**6. Language differences**
All languages run on top of it. Managed runtimes **reserve** large virtual ranges up front (the JVM reserves `-Xmx` worth of address space) but only touch pages as needed. A C buffer overflow can corrupt memory **within** its own process; protection only stops crossing into pages that are unmapped or forbidden.

**7. Practical example**

```c
int *p = NULL;
*p = 5;   // address 0 is never mapped → page fault → OS sends SIGSEGV → "Segmentation fault"
```

In Java the same mistake becomes a `NullPointerException`: the JVM catches the hardware fault and turns it into an exception.

**8. How can I observe it?**

- Windows Task Manager → Details: "Memory (private working set)" vs "Commit size"; Resource Monitor → "Hard Faults/sec".
- Linux: `cat /proc/<pid>/maps` (memory regions + permissions), `/usr/bin/time -v ./app` (page faults).

entries.question: What happens internally when we enter a URL and open a website?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?**
The browser turns a URL into a running page: find the server, connect securely, download HTML, then download and process everything the HTML needs.

**2. How does it work internally?**

1. **Parse the URL** — scheme, host, path. Check **HSTS** (force HTTPS) and the **HTTP cache**.
2. **DNS** — resolve `shop.com` to an IP (browser cache → OS → resolver).
3. **Connect** — TCP handshake + **TLS** handshake (or **QUIC** for HTTP/3, which combines both).
4. **Request** — `GET /` with headers and cookies.
5. **Response** — status, headers, HTML bytes (often compressed with gzip/brotli).
6. **Render** — the renderer parses HTML, finds CSS/JS/images and fetches them, builds the page and paints it.

**3. Visual**

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as You
  participant B as Browser process
  participant D as DNS resolver
  participant S as shop.com server
  participant R as Renderer process
  U->>B: types shop.com + Enter
  B->>B: HSTS + cache check
  B->>D: IP of shop.com?
  D-->>B: 93.184.216.34
  B->>S: TCP + TLS handshake
  B->>S: GET / (cookies)
  S-->>B: 200 OK + HTML
  B->>R: hand HTML to a renderer
  R->>S: GET app.css, main.js, logo.png
  R-->>U: pixels on screen
```

**4. Internal implementation**

- Chrome is **multi-process**: a **browser process** (UI, navigation), a **network service** (all HTTP), **renderer processes** (one per site, sandboxed), and a **GPU process**.
- The **preload scanner** reads ahead in the HTML to start downloading CSS/JS/images early, even while the main parser is blocked.
- Connections are reused (HTTP keep-alive, HTTP/2 multiplexing) so later requests skip the handshakes.

**5. Why is it designed this way?**
Separate processes isolate sites from each other (security) and keep one crashing tab from taking down the browser. Caching at every step (DNS, HTTP, connections) avoids repeating slow network round-trips.

**6. Framework differences**
A **server-rendered** page (Next.js, Spring MVC + Thymeleaf) arrives as ready HTML → fast first paint. A **single-page app** (Angular, React SPA) arrives as an almost empty HTML shell → content appears only after JavaScript downloads and runs.

**7. Practical example**
Opening an Angular app: `index.html` (~1 KB) → `main-HASH.js`, `polyfills-HASH.js`, `styles-HASH.css` → Angular bootstraps → calls `GET /api/products` → renders the product list.

**8. How can I observe it?**
Chrome DevTools → **Network** tab: click a request → **Timing** shows DNS, connect, SSL, waiting (TTFB) and download. `chrome://net-internals/#dns` shows the DNS cache.

entries.question: How do DOM, CSSOM, Render Tree, Layout and Paint work together?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?** The stages that turn parsed content into pixels: - **DOM** — what elements exist. **CSSOM** — which styles apply. - **Render tree / layout tree** — only the **visible** elements, each with its computed style. - **Layout** (reflow) — exact position and size of each box. - **Paint** — draw commands (text, colours, borders, images). - **Composite** — combine painted **layers** on the GPU into the final frame. **2. How does it work internally?** 1. **Style**: match CSS selectors to each DOM node → computed style. 2. **Layout tree**: skip `display: none` nodes and ``; add pseudo-elements like `::before`. 3. **Layout**: compute geometry top-down (a parent's width decides children's widths; children's heights decide the parent's height). 4. **Paint**: record display lists per layer. 5. **Raster + composite**: turn display lists into pixels (often on the GPU) and stack the layers. **3. Visual** ```mermaid flowchart LR DOM[DOM] --> S[Style] CSSOM[CSSOM] --> S S --> LT["Layout tree
(visible nodes only)"] LT --> L["Layout
x, y, width, height"] L --> P["Paint
display lists"] P --> R["Raster
tiles on GPU"] R --> C["Composite layers
→ frame"] ``` **4. Internal implementation** - Changing **geometry** (`width`, `top`, adding nodes) → layout + paint + composite (expensive). - Changing **only colours** (`color`, `background`) → paint + composite. - Changing **`transform` or `opacity`** on its own layer → **composite only** (cheap, runs on the compositor thread even when the main thread is busy). - **Layout thrashing**: reading `offsetHeight` right after writing styles forces a synchronous layout; doing it in a loop is very slow. **5. Why is it designed this way?** Separating stages lets the browser redo only the stages a change affects. Layers + a separate compositor thread keep scrolling and animations smooth at 60–120 fps. **6. Framework differences** Frameworks only change the **DOM**; the browser pipeline after that is identical. Good frameworks **batch** DOM writes to avoid repeated layouts. **7. Practical example** ```js // Slow: forces layout on every iteration items.forEach(el => { el.style.width = box.offsetWidth + "px"; }); // Fast: read once, then write const w = box.offsetWidth; items.forEach(el => { el.style.width = w + "px"; }); ``` **8. How can I observe it?** DevTools → **Performance**: purple = style/layout, green = paint. **Rendering** panel → "Paint flashing" (green flashes show repainted areas) and "Layer borders". **Layers** panel shows compositor layers.

entries.question: How does JavaScript execute inside a browser?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?** Each page runs its JavaScript on **one main thread** inside the renderer process, using the JS engine (V8, SpiderMonkey, JavaScriptCore). The same thread also does style, layout and paint, so long JavaScript blocks the page. **2. How does it work internally?** 1. The engine compiles the script (parse → bytecode; JIT for hot code). 2. It creates a **global execution context** (global object `window`, global scope). 3. Each function call creates an **execution context** pushed on the **call stack**: its scope, `this`, and arguments. 4. Before running a scope, the engine sets up its declarations: `function` declarations and `var` are **hoisted**; `let`/`const` exist but are in the **temporal dead zone** until their line runs. 5. Browser features (`setTimeout`, `fetch`, DOM events) are **Web APIs** provided by the browser, not the engine. **3. Visual** ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Renderer["Renderer process: main thread"] ENG["JS engine
call stack + heap"] REN["Rendering
style, layout, paint"] end API["Web APIs
timers, fetch, DOM events"] Q["Task + microtask queues"] ENG -- "calls" --> API API -- "callback when ready" --> Q Q -- "event loop" --> ENG ENG <-- "same thread, takes turns" --> REN ``` **4. Internal implementation** - **Scopes** are stored as context objects; closures keep a reference to the outer context, which is why captured variables stay alive. - DOM objects are C++ objects in the browser; JS gets **wrapper objects** that call into C++ (bindings). - Each tab/iframe origin has its own **realm** (separate globals) and the engine **isolate** owns the heap. **5. Why is it designed this way?** A single thread for DOM access means no locks or race conditions on the page. The cost: CPU-heavy JS freezes the UI, so heavy work belongs in Web Workers. **6. Language differences** TypeScript runs exactly like the JavaScript it compiles to. WebAssembly runs on the same main thread (unless in a worker) but can't touch the DOM directly — it calls JS for that. **7. Practical example** ```js console.log(typeof greet); // "function" (hoisted) console.log(x); // undefined (var hoisted, value not yet assigned) console.log(y); // ReferenceError (let: temporal dead zone) var x = 1; let y = 2; function greet() {} ``` **8. How can I observe it?** DevTools → **Sources**: breakpoints, **Call Stack** and **Scope** panels show execution contexts and closures. **Performance** → long yellow "Task" bars over 50 ms = UI-blocking JavaScript.

entries.question: How do Call Stack, Event Loop, Microtask Queue and Task Queue work?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?** - **Call stack** — the functions currently running. - **Task queue** (macrotasks) — callbacks from timers, events, network, `MessageChannel`. - **Microtask queue** — promise callbacks (`.then`, code after `await`), `queueMicrotask`, `MutationObserver`. - **Event loop** — the rule that decides what runs next. **2. How does it work internally?** One turn of the event loop: 1. Take the **oldest task** from a task queue and run it until the call stack is empty. 2. Run **all microtasks** — including ones added while running microtasks — until the queue is empty. 3. If it's time for a new frame (~16.7 ms at 60 Hz): run `requestAnimationFrame` callbacks, then style → layout → paint. 4. Repeat. **3. Visual** ```mermaid flowchart TD T["Run ONE task
(timer, click, network)"] --> M{"Microtasks
waiting?"} M -- yes --> RM["Run a microtask
(promise .then, await)"] --> M M -- no --> F{"Time to render
a frame?"} F -- yes --> R["rAF callbacks →
style → layout → paint"] --> T F -- no --> T ``` **4. Internal implementation** - Browsers have **several task queues** (input events, timers, networking) and may prioritise user input. - `setTimeout(fn, 0)` has a minimum delay (clamped to ≥4 ms after deep nesting) and runs as a **task**. - Microtasks run **before** rendering, so an endless chain of microtasks freezes the page just like an infinite loop. - Node.js has the same idea with phases (timers, poll, check) plus `process.nextTick`, which runs before promise microtasks. **5. Why is it designed this way?** Microtasks let promise chains finish **consistently** before anything else (no rendering half-way through an update). Tasks give other work (input, rendering) a chance between chunks. **6. Language differences** Python's `asyncio`, C#'s `async/await` and Java's `CompletableFuture` also use event loops or thread pools, but usually **multiple threads** exist. JavaScript's model is single-threaded per realm, so ordering is predictable. **7. Practical example** ```js console.log("1"); setTimeout(() => console.log("4"), 0); // task Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("3")); // microtask console.log("2"); // Output: 1 2 3 4 ``` **8. How can I observe it?** DevTools → **Performance** → each "Task" block, with "Run Microtasks" inside it. **loupe** (latentflip.com/loupe) visualises the stack and queues step by step.
entries.summary: Call stack — the functions currently running. Task queue (macrotasks) — callbacks from timers, events, network, MessageChannel. Microtask queue — promise callbacks (.then, code after await), queueMicrotask, MutationObserver. Event loop — the rule that decides what runs next.

entries.question: How does asynchronous JavaScript execute without blocking the UI?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?**
JavaScript starts slow work (network, timers, file reads) and **doesn't wait** for it. The browser does that work on **other threads**; when it finishes, a callback is queued and runs later on the main thread.

**2. How does it work internally?**

1. `fetch(url)` hands the request to the browser's **network service** (another process/thread) and immediately returns a **pending Promise**.
2. The main thread continues: handles clicks, renders frames.
3. When the response arrives, the network service queues a task that **resolves the promise**.
4. The promise's `.then` callbacks (or the code after `await`) run as **microtasks**.

**3. Visual**

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant M as Main thread (JS)
  participant N as Network thread
  participant Q as Queues
  M->>N: fetch("/api/orders")
  N-->>M: pending Promise (instantly)
  M->>M: keeps handling clicks + painting
  N->>Q: response ready → resolve promise
  Q->>M: microtask: code after await runs
```

**4. Internal implementation**

- `async` functions are compiled into **state machines**: each `await` saves local state, returns, and resumes in a microtask when the awaited promise settles.
- A Promise stores its state (pending/fulfilled/rejected), value, and a list of reactions to queue when it settles.
- **CPU-heavy** code is not made async by `async` — a long loop still blocks. Use **Web Workers** or split the work into chunks.

**5. Why is it designed this way?**
Most frontend work is waiting for I/O. Doing the waiting outside the main thread keeps one simple, lock-free thread for the UI.

**6. Language differences**

- **Java**: blocking I/O on a thread (or virtual threads); `CompletableFuture` for async.
- **C#**: `async/await` compiled to state machines too, continuations on a thread pool.
- **Python**: `asyncio` event loop, one thread, `await` like JS.
- **Go**: write blocking code; the runtime parks the goroutine and runs others.

**7. Practical example**

```js
async function load() {
  spinner.show();
  const res = await fetch("/api/orders");   // main thread is free while waiting
  render(await res.json());
  spinner.hide();
}
```

**8. How can I observe it?**
DevTools → **Network** (request timing) together with **Performance** (main thread idle while the request is in flight). Throttle the network to "Slow 3G" and confirm the page still scrolls.

entries.question: How does a browser determine which UI elements need updating?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?**
The browser tracks **what changed** and redoes only the necessary work for those parts, instead of re-rendering the whole page every frame.

**2. How does it work internally?**

1. A DOM or style change marks the affected nodes **dirty** (e.g. "style needs recalc", "needs layout").
2. At the next frame, **style recalc** runs only for dirty nodes (and descendants affected by inheritance or selectors).
3. **Layout** runs for dirty subtrees; containment can stop it spreading.
4. **Paint invalidation** marks changed rectangles; only those are repainted.
5. The **compositor** re-combines layers; transform/opacity changes skip steps 2–4.

**3. Visual**

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  CH["JS changes the page"] --> K{What changed?}
  K -- "transform / opacity" --> CO[Composite only]
  K -- "color / background" --> PA["Paint dirty area → composite"]
  K -- "size / position / DOM nodes" --> LA["Layout dirty subtree → paint → composite"]
  K -- "class names" --> ST["Style recalc for matching nodes → ..."]
```

**4. Internal implementation**

- Dirty **bits/flags** on nodes; Blink's "invalidation sets" track which selectors a class change can affect.
- CSS `contain: layout paint` and `content-visibility: auto` tell the browser a subtree is independent, so changes inside don't relayout the rest.
- Raster **tiles**: only tiles covering changed areas are re-rasterised.

**5. Why is it designed this way?**
Redoing everything 60+ times a second is impossible on big pages. Incremental invalidation keeps cost proportional to the size of the change.

**6. Framework differences**
Frameworks decide **which DOM nodes to touch** (next question); the browser then decides **which rendering work** those touches require. Both layers try to do the minimum.

**7. Practical example**
Animating `left: 0 → 300px` relayouts every frame. Animating `transform: translateX(300px)` is composite-only → smooth even if JavaScript is busy.

**8. How can I observe it?**
DevTools → **Rendering** → "Paint flashing" and "Layout Shift Regions"; **Performance** → "Recalculate Style" shows how many elements were affected.

entries.question: How do Angular, React and Vue detect changes and update the DOM?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?** Each framework must answer: "the data changed — which DOM nodes must change?" They use three different strategies. **2. How does it work internally?** - **Angular (zone.js default)** — after any async event, walk the component tree **top-down** and compare each template binding's current value with the previous one; update the DOM where they differ. With **Signals**, only views that read a changed signal are marked for checking. - **React** — calling `setState` re-runs the component function → new **virtual DOM** → **diff** against the previous one → apply the minimal DOM changes. - **Vue** — data is wrapped in **Proxies** that record which component reads which property; a change re-renders only those components (then a virtual DOM diff inside them). **3. Visual** ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph Angular A1["Event (zone.js) or signal change"] --> A2["Check bindings top-down
(skip OnPush/clean views)"] --> A3[Update changed DOM bindings] end subgraph React R1["setState"] --> R2["Re-render component + children
→ new virtual DOM"] --> R3["Diff old vs new"] --> R4[Commit DOM changes] end subgraph Vue V1["state.count++ (Proxy set)"] --> V2["Find components that read 'count'"] --> V3["Re-render those → diff"] --> V4[Patch DOM] end ``` **4. Internal implementation** | | Angular | React | Vue | |---|---|---|---| | Knows **what** changed? | No (zone) / Yes (Signals) | No — re-renders and diffs | Yes — Proxy tracking | | Unit of re-check | Template bindings | Component subtree | Component | | DOM update | Direct binding updates (no virtual DOM) | Virtual DOM diff | Virtual DOM diff with compiler hints | **5. Why is it designed this way?** Angular's dirty checking is simple and works with plain objects; React's "re-render everything + diff" gives a simple mental model (UI = f(state)); Vue's tracking avoids unnecessary re-renders automatically. All three are moving toward **fine-grained reactivity** (Angular Signals, Vue Vapor mode, React Compiler auto-memoisation). **6. Framework differences** Svelte and SolidJS skip the virtual DOM: their compiler or signals update exact DOM nodes. See the framework internals notes for each framework in depth. **7. Practical example** A counter increments: Angular checks the bindings in the counter's view (and others in the checked path); React re-runs `Counter()` and diffs; Vue re-runs only `Counter`'s render because only it read `count`. **8. How can I observe it?** **Angular DevTools** → Profiler (change detection cycles), **React DevTools** → Profiler + "Highlight updates", **Vue DevTools** → Timeline / component re-render events.
entries.summary: What is it? Each framework must answer: "the data changed — which DOM nodes must change?" They use three different strategies.

codeBlocks.code:
flowchart TB subgraph Angular A1["Event (zone.js) or signal change"] --> A2["Check bindings top-down
(skip OnPush/clean views)"] --> A3[Update changed DOM bindings] end subgraph React R1["setState"] --> R2["Re-render component + children
→ new virtual DOM"] --> R3["Diff old vs new"] --> R4[Commit DOM changes] end subgraph Vue V1["state.count++ (Proxy set)"] --> V2["Find components that read 'count'"] --> V3["Re-render those → diff"] --> V4[Patch DOM] end

entries.question: How does a frontend application communicate with a backend?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?**
The frontend sends **HTTP requests** (usually JSON over HTTPS) to backend APIs and updates the UI with the responses. For live updates it can keep a connection open (WebSocket, Server-Sent Events).

**2. How does it work internally?**

1. Code calls `fetch` / `HttpClient` / `axios` → the browser builds an HTTP request.
2. If the API is on another **origin**, the browser applies **CORS**: non-simple requests first send an `OPTIONS` **preflight**; the server must answer with `Access-Control-Allow-*` headers.
3. Cookies for that site are attached automatically (if allowed); tokens go in the `Authorization` header by your code.
4. The request travels over a reused HTTPS connection (HTTP/2 or HTTP/3).
5. The backend responds; JS parses the body (`res.json()`), updates state, the framework updates the DOM.

**3. Visual**

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant UI as Angular app (app.shop.com)
  participant BR as Browser
  participant API as api.shop.com
  UI->>BR: http.post('/orders', body)
  BR->>API: OPTIONS /orders (CORS preflight)
  API-->>BR: 204 Access-Control-Allow-Origin: app.shop.com
  BR->>API: POST /orders + Authorization: Bearer ...
  API-->>BR: 201 Created + JSON
  BR-->>UI: Observable emits the order
```

**4. Internal implementation**

- `fetch` and `XMLHttpRequest` are Web APIs; the network service does DNS, connection pooling, TLS, HTTP framing and caching.
- JSON is serialised with `JSON.stringify` and parsed with `JSON.parse` — structured data becomes UTF-8 text on the wire.
- CORS is enforced **by the browser**, not the server: the server only sends permission headers.

**5. Why is it designed this way?**
HTTP + JSON is universal, cacheable and easy to debug. The same-origin policy + CORS stops a malicious site from reading your bank's API with your cookies.

**6. Framework differences**
Angular `HttpClient` returns cold **Observables** (nothing is sent until you subscribe) with interceptors; React/Vue usually use `fetch`/axios with Promises (plus libraries like TanStack Query for caching). All use the same browser networking underneath.

**7. Practical example**

```ts
this.http.get<Order[]>('/api/orders').subscribe(orders => this.orders = orders);
```

**8. How can I observe it?**
DevTools → **Network** → Fetch/XHR filter: headers, preflight requests, payload, response, timing. CORS errors appear in the **Console**.
entries.summary: What is it? The frontend sends HTTP requests (usually JSON over HTTPS) to backend APIs and updates the UI with the responses. For live updates it can keep a connection open (WebSocket, Server-Sent Events).

  participant BR as Browser
  participant API as api.shop.com
  UI->>BR: http.post('/orders', body)
  BR->>API: OPTIONS /orders (CORS preflight)
  API-->>BR: 204 Access-Control-Allow-Origin: app.shop.com
  BR->>API: POST /orders + Authorization: Bearer ...
  API-->>BR: 201 Created + JSON
  BR-->>UI: Observable emits the order
this.http.get<Order[]>('/api/orders').subscribe(orders => this.orders = orders);

entries.question: How do bundlers, Tree Shaking and Code Splitting work?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?** - **Bundler** (Vite/Rollup, esbuild, webpack, Angular CLI) — follows `import` statements from your entry file and combines modules into a few optimised files. - **Tree shaking** — removes exports nobody imports. - **Code splitting** — splits the bundle into **chunks** loaded only when needed. **2. How does it work internally?** 1. Start at the entry (`main.ts`), parse it, find `import`s, and build a **module graph**. 2. Transform each module (TypeScript → JS, JSX → JS, CSS imports). 3. **Tree shake**: mark which exports are used; unused ones are dropped (if the module has no side effects). 4. **Split**: each dynamic `import()` starts a new chunk; shared code goes into common chunks. 5. **Minify** (rename variables, remove whitespace and dead code) and add **content hashes** to file names (`main-3f9a.js`) for caching. **3. Visual** ```mermaid flowchart LR E[main.ts] --> A[app.component.ts] E --> U["utils.ts
format() used, parse() unused"] A -. "import() dynamic" .-> AD["admin.module.ts"] subgraph Output["dist/"] M["main-3f9a.js
app + format()"] C["chunk-admin-91bc.js
loaded on /admin"] end E --> M AD --> C U -. "parse() removed" .-> X[tree-shaken] ``` **4. Internal implementation** - Tree shaking needs **static ES module syntax** (`import`/`export`): imports are known at build time. CommonJS `require()` is dynamic and harder to shake. - `"sideEffects": false` in a library's `package.json` tells the bundler unused files are safe to drop. - Dynamic `import()` compiles to code that fetches the chunk file and returns a Promise of the module. **5. Why is it designed this way?** Less JavaScript = faster download, parse and execution, especially on mobile. Hashed file names allow "cache forever" headers because any change produces a new name. **6. Framework differences** Angular CLI (esbuild-based application builder) splits per lazy route automatically; Vite uses esbuild in dev and Rollup for production builds (newer versions move to Rolldown); Next.js splits per page automatically. **7. Practical example** ```ts { path: 'admin', loadComponent: () => import('./admin/admin.component').then(m => m.AdminComponent) } ``` The admin code is a separate chunk downloaded only when the user opens `/admin`. **8. How can I observe it?** `ng build --stats-json` or `npx vite build`, then **source-map-explorer** or **esbuild Bundle Analyzer** / `rollup-plugin-visualizer`. DevTools → **Network**: navigate to `/admin` and watch the new chunk load. **Coverage** tab shows unused bytes.
entries.summary: Bundler (Vite/Rollup, esbuild, webpack, Angular CLI) — follows import statements from your entry file and combines modules into a few optimised files. Tree shaking — removes exports nobody imports. Code splitting — splits the bundle into chunks loaded only when needed.

format() used, parse() unused"] A -. "import() dynamic" .-> AD["admin.module.ts"] subgraph Output["dist/"] M["main-3f9a.js
app + format()"] C["chunk-admin-91bc.js
loaded on /admin"] end E --> M AD --> C U -. "parse() removed" .-> X[tree-shaken]

entries.question: How do Browser Cache, Cookies, LocalStorage, SessionStorage and IndexedDB work?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?** Five ways a browser keeps data, all **separated per origin** (scheme + host + port): | Storage | Holds | Size (approx.) | Sent to server? | Lifetime | |---|---|---|---|---| | **HTTP cache** | Responses (JS, CSS, images, API) | Hundreds of MB | No (it replaces requests) | By `Cache-Control` / eviction | | **Cookies** | Small key=value strings | ~4 KB each | **Yes, with every matching request** | Session or `Expires` | | **LocalStorage** | Strings | ~5–10 MB | No | Until cleared | | **SessionStorage** | Strings | ~5 MB | No | Until the **tab** closes | | **IndexedDB** | Structured data, files, blobs | Large (% of disk) | No | Until cleared / evicted | **2. How does it work internally?** - **HTTP cache**: keyed by URL (+ some headers); fresh → used without a request; stale → revalidated with `ETag`/`If-None-Match` (304). - **Cookies**: stored by the browser; `Set-Cookie` creates them; attributes `HttpOnly` (no JS access), `Secure` (HTTPS only), `SameSite` (cross-site rules). - **LocalStorage/SessionStorage**: simple **synchronous** key-value maps on disk/memory; reads block the main thread. - **IndexedDB**: an **asynchronous**, transactional database of object stores with indexes; values copied with the structured clone algorithm. **3. Visual** ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph Origin["Origin: https://shop.com"] HC[(HTTP cache)] CK[(Cookies)] LS[(LocalStorage)] SS[("SessionStorage
per tab")] IDB[(IndexedDB)] end REQ[Every request to shop.com] -- "auto-attached" --> CK JS[JavaScript] --> LS JS --> SS JS -- "async transactions" --> IDB NET[Network fetch] -- "check first" --> HC ``` **4. Internal implementation** - Chrome stores the HTTP cache in disk cache files + an in-memory cache; LocalStorage and IndexedDB live in per-origin storage (LevelDB/SQLite depending on browser). - Storage is **partitioned**: third-party iframes get separate storage per top-level site (privacy). - Under storage pressure, browsers evict "best-effort" origins unless `navigator.storage.persist()` was granted. **5. Why is it designed this way?** Cookies exist for server sessions (sent automatically). Web Storage gives simple client-side persistence. IndexedDB handles large offline data without blocking the UI. Separation by origin prevents sites reading each other's data. **6. Framework differences** Same browser APIs for all frameworks. Security note: storing JWTs in LocalStorage exposes them to XSS; `HttpOnly` cookies can't be read by JS. **7. Practical example** Angular app: refresh token in an `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict` cookie, UI theme in LocalStorage, form draft in SessionStorage, offline product catalogue in IndexedDB. **8. How can I observe it?** DevTools → **Application** tab: Cookies, Local/Session Storage, IndexedDB, Cache Storage, and "Storage" usage per origin. **Network** → "Size" column shows "(disk cache)" / "(memory cache)".
entries.summary: What is it? Five ways a browser keeps data, all separated per origin (scheme + host + port):

codeBlocks.code:
flowchart TB subgraph Origin["Origin: https://shop.com"] HC[(HTTP cache)] CK[(Cookies)] LS[(LocalStorage)] SS[("SessionStorage
per tab")] IDB[(IndexedDB)] end REQ[Every request to shop.com] -- "auto-attached" --> CK JS[JavaScript] --> LS JS --> SS JS -- "async transactions" --> IDB NET[Network fetch] -- "check first" --> HC

entries.question: How do Browser Tabs and Web Workers work internally?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?** - **Tabs** — modern browsers run sites in separate **renderer processes**, each with its own main thread, JS heap and event loop. - **Web Workers** — extra **threads** inside a page that run JavaScript in the background, with their own event loop and no DOM access. **2. How does it work internally?** 1. Opening a tab: the browser process assigns a sandboxed renderer process (**site isolation**: different sites → different processes). 2. `new Worker('worker.js')` starts an OS thread with a separate JS **isolate** (own heap, own globals). 3. Page and worker talk only by **`postMessage`**; data is copied with **structured clone** (or moved with **transferables** like `ArrayBuffer`, without copying). 4. **SharedArrayBuffer** + `Atomics` allow real shared memory (requires cross-origin isolation headers). **3. Visual** ```mermaid flowchart TB BP["Browser process
tabs UI, navigation"] --> R1["Renderer: shop.com
main thread + JS heap"] BP --> R2["Renderer: bank.com
main thread + JS heap"] BP --> GPU[GPU process] BP --> NET[Network service] R1 --> W1["Web Worker thread
own heap + event loop"] R1 <-- "postMessage (copy / transfer)" --> W1 SW["Service Worker
proxy between page and network"] --- R1 ``` **4. Internal implementation** - Renderer processes are **sandboxed**: they can't open files or sockets directly; they ask the browser process via IPC. - Worker types: **Dedicated** (one page), **Shared** (several pages of the same origin), **Service Worker** (intercepts network requests, enables offline and push notifications). - Background tabs get **timer throttling** and may be frozen to save battery. **5. Why is it designed this way?** Process isolation stops a malicious page reading another site's memory (important after Spectre) and contains crashes. Workers give parallelism without the dangers of shared-memory threads on the DOM. **6. Language differences** JavaScript workers are like threads that share **nothing** by default (actor-style), unlike Java/C#/C++ threads that share the whole heap. Node.js has the same model with `worker_threads`. **7. Practical example** ```js // main.js const w = new Worker('resize.js'); w.postMessage(imageBuffer, [imageBuffer]); // transfer, no copy w.onmessage = e => show(e.data); // resize.js onmessage = e => postMessage(resize(e.data)); // heavy work off the main thread ``` **8. How can I observe it?** Chrome **Task Manager** (Shift+Esc) shows processes per tab/site; `chrome://process-internals`. DevTools → **Sources** → Threads panel lists workers; **Application** → Service Workers.
entries.summary: Tabs — modern browsers run sites in separate renderer processes, each with its own main thread, JS heap and event loop. Web Workers — extra threads inside a page that run JavaScript in the background, with their own event loop and no DOM access.

codeBlocks.code:
flowchart TB BP["Browser process
tabs UI, navigation"] --> R1["Renderer: shop.com
main thread + JS heap"] BP --> R2["Renderer: bank.com
main thread + JS heap"] BP --> GPU[GPU process] BP --> NET[Network service] R1 --> W1["Web Worker thread
own heap + event loop"] R1 <-- "postMessage (copy / transfer)" --> W1 SW["Service Worker
proxy between page and network"] --- R1

entries.question: How do Angular application bootstrap and compilation work internally?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?** **Compilation** turns component templates into JavaScript functions at build time (AOT). **Bootstrap** is what happens in the browser when `main.ts` starts the app and renders the root component. **2. How does it work internally?** Build time: 1. The Angular compiler reads `@Component` metadata and the HTML template. 2. It generates a **template function** per component made of Ivy instructions (`ɵɵelementStart`, `ɵɵtext`, `ɵɵproperty`…) with two modes: **create** (build DOM once) and **update** (refresh bindings). 3. The bundler outputs `main-HASH.js`. Runtime: 4. `bootstrapApplication(AppComponent, appConfig)` creates the **platform injector** and the root **environment injector** with your providers. 5. Angular finds `` in `index.html`, creates `AppComponent`, runs its template function in **create** mode. 6. It runs the first **change detection** (update mode) and attaches listeners; after that it reacts to events or signals. **3. Visual** ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Build["Build time (ng build)"] T["app.component.html
+ .ts metadata"] --> C["Angular compiler (AOT)"] --> F["template function
Ivy instructions"] --> B["main-HASH.js"] end subgraph Browser["Runtime (browser)"] M["main.ts:
bootstrapApplication()"] --> I["Create injectors
platform + root"] --> R["Create AppComponent
in app-root"] R --> CR["Template fn: create mode
→ real DOM"] --> CD["First change detection
update mode"] end B --> M ``` **4. Internal implementation** - Each component instance has an **LView** (an array holding its DOM nodes, binding values and child views) and a shared **TView** (the static template blueprint). - Bindings are stored at fixed indexes in the LView, so an update compares `oldValue !== newValue` per slot. - No virtual DOM: instructions update real DOM nodes directly. **5. Why is it designed this way?** AOT finds template errors at build time, removes the compiler from the bundle and enables **tree shaking** of unused Angular features (Ivy's "locality": each component compiles independently). Cost: build step required; templates can't be built dynamically from strings at runtime. **6. Framework differences** React compiles only JSX syntax (to function calls) and decides the DOM at runtime via a virtual DOM; Vue compiles templates to render functions with optimisation hints; Svelte compiles to direct DOM code like Angular but without a change detection pass. **7. Practical example** ```html

Hello {{ name }}

``` compiles roughly to: create mode → `ɵɵelementStart(0,'h1'); ɵɵtext(1); ɵɵelementEnd()`; update mode → `ɵɵtextInterpolate1('Hello ', ctx.name, '')`. **8. How can I observe it?** `ng build --configuration development` and open `dist/.../main.js`: search for `ɵɵ` to see template functions. **Angular DevTools** → Components shows the tree created at bootstrap.
entries.summary: What is it? Compilation turns component templates into JavaScript functions at build time (AOT). Bootstrap is what happens in the browser when main.ts starts the app and renders the root component.

Ivy instructions"] --> B["main-HASH.js"] end subgraph Browser["Runtime (browser)"] M["main.ts:
bootstrapApplication()"] --> I["Create injectors

entries.question: How does Angular Dependency Injection work internally?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?** Angular creates and hands out objects (services) for you. A class **asks** for what it needs (`inject(UserService)` or a constructor parameter); an **injector** finds or creates it. **2. How does it work internally?** 1. Every **token** (a class or `InjectionToken`) maps to a **provider** recipe: `useClass`, `useValue`, `useFactory`, `useExisting`. 2. Resolution walks **up** a hierarchy: the component's **element injector** → parent elements → the **environment injector** (route / lazy / root) → platform → `NullInjector` (error: "No provider for X"). 3. The first injector that has a provider creates the instance (once, then caches it) and returns it. **3. Visual** ```mermaid flowchart BT C["ProductCard component
element injector"] --> P["ProductList component
element injector"] P --> L["Lazy route injector
(providers: [CartService])"] L --> R["Root environment injector
providedIn: 'root' services"] R --> PL[Platform injector] PL --> N["NullInjector → error"] ``` **4. Internal implementation** - The compiler generates a **factory** per injectable (`ɵfac`) that calls `inject()` for each dependency. - Injectors store records in a map `token → {factory, value}`; cycles are detected (`NG0200: Circular dependency`). - `providedIn: 'root'` services are **tree-shakable**: if nothing injects them, they are not bundled. - Element injectors are stored in the LView using a **bloom filter** to quickly skip elements that can't provide a token. **5. Why is it designed this way?** Loose coupling and easy testing (swap a real `HttpClient` for a mock). The hierarchy lets a feature or component get its **own** instance (scoped state). Cost: misconfigured providers can create unexpected duplicate instances. **6. Framework differences** | Framework | DI | |---|---| | Angular | Full hierarchical injector system, built in | | Spring (Java) | Container-wide singletons by default, created at start-up | | ASP.NET Core | Built-in container with singleton / scoped (per request) / transient lifetimes | | React / Vue | No DI container; **Context** / `provide`-`inject` pass values down the tree | **7. Practical example** ```ts @Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' }) export class CartService { items = signal([]); } @Component({ ... }) export class CartIcon { cart = inject(CartService); } // same root instance everywhere ``` **8. How can I observe it?** **Angular DevTools** → select a component → "Injected services" and the **Injector Tree** view (Angular 17+). Add `providers: [CartService]` to a component and watch a second instance appear.
entries.summary: What is it? Angular creates and hands out objects (services) for you. A class asks for what it needs (inject(UserService) or a constructor parameter); an injector finds or creates it.

element injector"] --> P["ProductList component
element injector"] P --> L["Lazy route injector
(providers: [CartService])"] L --> R["Root environment injector
providedIn: 'root' services"] R --> PL[Platform injector] PL --> N["NullInjector → error"]

entries.question: How does the Angular component lifecycle work internally?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?** Angular calls **lifecycle hooks** on a component at fixed moments: when it is created, when its inputs change, after its view is checked, and before it is destroyed. **2. How does it work internally?** Order for one component: 1. `constructor` — class created (DI happens here). No inputs yet. 2. `ngOnChanges` — inputs set or changed (before `ngOnInit` and on every input change). 3. `ngOnInit` — once, after the first inputs. 4. `ngDoCheck` — every change detection run. 5. `ngAfterContentInit` / `ngAfterContentChecked` — projected `` ready / checked. 6. `ngAfterViewInit` / `ngAfterViewChecked` — own view and children ready / checked. 7. `ngOnDestroy` — before removal (clean up subscriptions, timers). **3. Visual** ```mermaid flowchart TD CT[constructor] --> OC["ngOnChanges
(if inputs)"] --> OI["ngOnInit (once)"] --> DC[ngDoCheck] DC --> ACI["ngAfterContentInit (once)"] --> ACC[ngAfterContentChecked] ACC --> AVI["ngAfterViewInit (once)"] --> AVC[ngAfterViewChecked] AVC -. "each later change detection:
ngOnChanges if inputs changed, ngDoCheck,
AfterContentChecked, AfterViewChecked" .-> DC AVC --> OD["ngOnDestroy (on removal)"] ``` **4. Internal implementation** - Hooks are registered in the component's **TView** as arrays (`preOrderHooks`, `contentHooks`, `viewHooks`, `destroyHooks`) at first creation. - During **refreshView**, Angular runs: pre-order hooks (OnChanges/OnInit/DoCheck) → update bindings → content hooks → refresh child views → view hooks. - `ngOnChanges` receives a `SimpleChanges` object built by comparing previous and current input values. - Newer APIs `afterNextRender` / `afterRender` run after the DOM is rendered (useful for measuring elements). **5. Why is it designed this way?** Hooks tie into the change detection walk, so they cost nothing extra and run in a predictable order (parents before children for init, children before parents for view hooks). **6. Framework differences** React uses `useEffect` (after paint), `useLayoutEffect` (before paint) and cleanup functions instead of named hooks. Vue has `onMounted`, `onUpdated`, `onUnmounted` and friends — similar idea to Angular. **7. Practical example** ```ts export class PriceTicker implements OnInit, OnDestroy { private sub?: Subscription; ngOnInit() { this.sub = interval(1000).subscribe(() => this.refresh()); } ngOnDestroy() { this.sub?.unsubscribe(); } // without this: memory leak } ``` **8. How can I observe it?** Add `console.log` in each hook and toggle the component with `@if`. **Angular DevTools** → Profiler shows which hooks ran and how long they took.
entries.summary: What is it? Angular calls lifecycle hooks on a component at fixed moments: when it is created, when its inputs change, after its view is checked, and before it is destroyed.

flowchart TD CT[constructor] --> OC["ngOnChanges
(if inputs)"] --> OI["ngOnInit (once)"] --> DC[ngDoCheck] DC --> ACI["ngAfterContentInit (once)"] --> ACC[ngAfterContentChecked] ACC --> AVI["ngAfterViewInit (once)"] --> AVC[ngAfterViewChecked] AVC -. "each later change detection:
ngOnChanges if inputs changed, ngDoCheck,
AfterContentChecked, AfterViewChecked" .-> DC AVC --> OD["ngOnDestroy (on removal)"]

entries.question: How do Angular Change Detection and Signals work internally?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?** Change detection keeps the DOM in sync with component data. Angular has two triggers: **zone.js** (classic: "something async happened, check everything") and **Signals** (reactive: "this value changed, update what reads it"). **2. How does it work internally?** Zone-based: 1. **zone.js** patches async APIs (events, `setTimeout`, promises, XHR). 2. When one finishes, `ApplicationRef.tick()` runs. 3. Angular walks the view tree **top-down**, running each template function in update mode and comparing every binding with its previous value. 4. `OnPush` components are skipped unless an input reference changed, an event fired inside them, an `async` pipe emitted, or they were marked dirty. Signals: 1. A `signal()` is a **producer**; templates, `computed()` and `effect()` that read it become **consumers** (dependencies are recorded automatically). 2. Setting a signal marks its consumers **dirty**; a template consumer marks its view for refresh. 3. In **zoneless** mode (`provideZonelessChangeDetection()`, stable from Angular 20), Angular schedules a check only when signals, events or `markForCheck` say something changed. **3. Visual** ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph Zone["zone.js mode"] E[click / timer / HTTP] --> Z[zone.js] --> T["ApplicationRef.tick()"] --> W["Walk all views top-down
(skip clean OnPush)"] end subgraph Sig["Signals mode"] S["count.set(5)"] --> G["Reactive graph:
mark consumers dirty"] --> V["Only views that read 'count'
are refreshed"] end W --> D[Update changed DOM bindings] V --> D ``` **4. Internal implementation** - Bindings live at fixed slots in each view's LView; update = `if (!Object.is(old, new)) setDomProperty(...)`. - In dev mode a second check pass runs and throws **`ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenCheckedError`** if a binding changed during the check. - Signals use **version numbers**: a `computed` recomputes lazily only if a dependency's version changed (push "dirty", pull value). **5. Why is it designed this way?** Zone.js made change detection automatic with plain objects, but checks far more than needed and adds a dependency. Signals give **fine-grained** updates, better performance and no zone.js — at the cost of writing state as signals. **6. Framework differences** React re-renders component functions and diffs a virtual DOM; Vue tracks property reads with Proxies; SolidJS and Preact Signals use the same producer/consumer idea as Angular Signals. **7. Practical example** ```ts count = signal(0); double = computed(() => this.count() * 2); // recomputed only when count changes inc() { this.count.update(c => c + 1); } // marks only this component's view dirty ``` ```html

{{ count() }} × 2 = {{ double() }}

``` **8. How can I observe it?** **Angular DevTools** → Profiler: record, click around, see each change detection cycle and which components were checked. Compare a zone app with a zoneless + Signals app.

entries.question: How do the Angular Router and lazy loading work internally?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?** The **Router** maps the browser URL to components. **Lazy loading** downloads a route's code only when the user first navigates to it. **2. How does it work internally?** 1. Navigation starts (link click, `router.navigate`, or browser back/forward via the `popstate` event). 2. The URL is parsed into a **UrlTree**. 3. **Route matching**: the router walks the route config to find matching routes (and params like `:id`). 4. For lazy routes, `loadComponent` / `loadChildren` runs a dynamic `import()` → the chunk is fetched. 5. **Guards** (`canActivate`, `canMatch`…) and **resolvers** run. 6. The router creates components in the matching ``s and updates the address bar with `history.pushState` (no page reload). **3. Visual** ```mermaid flowchart LR N["Click /admin/users"] --> P[Parse to UrlTree] --> MA[Match route config] MA --> LZ{"Lazy route?"} LZ -- yes --> IM["import() → fetch chunk-admin.js"] --> G LZ -- no --> G["Guards + resolvers"] G -- allowed --> A["Activate: create components
in router-outlet"] A --> H["history.pushState
URL updated, no reload"] G -- denied --> X[Cancel or redirect] ``` **4. Internal implementation** - Router state is a tree of **ActivatedRoute** objects (params, data, query params as Observables/signals). - Navigation is an RxJS pipeline; a new navigation **cancels** an unfinished one. - Lazy route configs are cached after the first load; **preloading strategies** (e.g. `PreloadAllModules`) fetch chunks in the background after start-up. **5. Why is it designed this way?** SPA navigation without reloads is fast and keeps state. Lazy loading keeps the first download small; a large admin area doesn't slow down the home page. **6. Framework differences** React Router / TanStack Router and Vue Router follow the same pattern (route table + `history.pushState` + `import()` for lazy routes). Next.js and Nuxt use **file-based routing** and split code per page automatically. **7. Practical example** ```ts export const routes: Routes = [ { path: '', component: HomeComponent }, { path: 'admin', canMatch: [adminGuard], loadChildren: () => import('./admin/admin.routes').then(m => m.ADMIN_ROUTES) }, ]; ``` **8. How can I observe it?** DevTools → **Network** → JS filter: navigate to `/admin` and see the chunk load once. `provideRouter(routes, withDebugTracing())` logs every router event (NavigationStart, GuardsCheck, NavigationEnd).
entries.summary: What is it? The Router maps the browser URL to components. Lazy loading downloads a route's code only when the user first navigates to it.

entries.question: How do Angular HttpClient and HTTP Interceptors work internally?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?** `HttpClient` sends HTTP requests and returns **Observables**. **Interceptors** are functions that every request and response pass through — for auth headers, logging, retries, error handling. **2. How does it work internally?** 1. `http.get('/api/orders')` creates an immutable **HttpRequest** and returns a **cold Observable** — nothing is sent yet. 2. On `subscribe` (or `async` pipe / `toSignal`), the request enters the **interceptor chain** in the order provided. 3. Each interceptor can clone and modify the request, then call `next(req)`. 4. The last handler, **HttpBackend**, sends it using `XMLHttpRequest` (default) or `fetch` (`withFetch()`). 5. The response flows back **through the interceptors in reverse**, as `HttpEvent`s, then to your subscriber. **3. Visual** ```mermaid flowchart LR C["Component
http.get()"] -- subscribe --> I1["authInterceptor
add Bearer token"] I1 --> I2["loggingInterceptor"] I2 --> BE["HttpBackend
XHR or fetch"] BE --> API[(Backend API)] API --> BE BE -- response --> I2 -- response --> I1 I1 -- "401? refresh + retry" --> C ``` **4. Internal implementation** - Requests and headers are **immutable**; interceptors use `req.clone({ setHeaders: {...} })`. - Functional interceptors (`HttpInterceptorFn`) are registered with `provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([...]))` and can use `inject()`. - Unsubscribing **aborts** the underlying XHR/fetch, so `switchMap` cancels outdated searches automatically. - JSON is parsed by the backend handler based on `responseType`. **5. Why is it designed this way?** Observables give cancellation, retries (`retry`), and composition with RxJS. The interceptor chain (Chain of Responsibility pattern) keeps cross-cutting concerns out of every service. **6. Framework differences** React/Vue apps usually use `fetch` or **axios** (axios has request/response interceptors too). Spring's `RestClient`/`WebClient` and OkHttp on the backend use the same interceptor-chain idea. **7. Practical example** ```ts export const authInterceptor: HttpInterceptorFn = (req, next) => { const token = inject(AuthService).token(); return next(token ? req.clone({ setHeaders: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } }) : req); }; ``` **8. How can I observe it?** DevTools → **Network**: confirm the `Authorization` header. Calling `http.get()` without subscribing sends **nothing** — a quick way to see the Observable is cold.
entries.summary: What is it? HttpClient sends HTTP requests and returns Observables. Interceptors are functions that every request and response pass through — for auth headers, logging, retries, error handling.

XHR or fetch"] BE --> API[(Backend API)] API --> BE BE -- response --> I2 -- response --> I1 I1 -- "401? refresh + retry" --> C

entries.question: How do React's Virtual DOM and Reconciliation work internally?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?** A component returns a description of the UI as plain JavaScript objects (**React elements**, the "virtual DOM"). **Reconciliation** compares the new description with the previous one and changes only the real DOM nodes that differ. **2. How does it work internally?** 1. State changes → React calls the component function again → new element tree. 2. React compares old and new **node by node**: - Different **type** (`div` → `span`, `A` → `B`) → destroy the old subtree, build a new one. - Same type → keep the DOM node / component instance, update changed props. - Lists → match children by **`key`**; without keys, by position. 3. The resulting changes are applied to the DOM in the **commit** phase. **3. Visual** ```mermaid flowchart TD S["setState"] --> R["Call Component()
→ new element tree"] R --> D{"Same type as before?"} D -- no --> RE[Unmount old subtree, mount new] D -- yes --> UP["Keep node, diff props"] UP --> K["Diff children
match by key"] RE --> CM["Commit: apply DOM mutations"] K --> CM ``` **4. Internal implementation** - A React element is `{ type, props, key, ref }` — cheap to create. - The diff is **O(n)** thanks to two heuristics (different type = different tree; keys identify list items). A general tree diff would be O(n³). - Using **array index as key** in a reorderable list makes React reuse the wrong DOM nodes (inputs keep the wrong values). **5. Why is it designed this way?** Developers describe the UI for the current state (`UI = f(state)`) and never write DOM update code. The cost: React re-runs components and diffs even when little changed — mitigated by `memo`, `useMemo` and the React Compiler. **6. Framework differences** Vue also diffs a virtual DOM but knows **which components** depend on changed data and uses compiler hints to skip static parts. Angular, Svelte and Solid have **no virtual DOM**. **7. Practical example** ```jsx {todos.map(t => )} ``` Removing the first todo: with `key={t.id}` React removes one row; with `key={index}` it would update every row's props and delete the last one. **8. How can I observe it?** **React DevTools** → Profiler: record an update to see which components rendered and why. Settings → "Highlight updates when components render".
entries.summary: What is it? A component returns a description of the UI as plain JavaScript objects (React elements, the "virtual DOM"). Reconciliation compares the new description with the previous one and changes only the real DOM nodes that differ.
