entries.question: How does Distributed Tracing track a request across multiple services?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?**
**Distributed tracing** follows one request through every service it touches. The whole journey is a **trace**; each unit of work (an HTTP call, a DB query) is a **span** with a start time, duration and parent. All spans share one **trace ID**.

**2. How does it work internally?**

1. The first service (or gateway) starts a trace: random **trace ID** + a root **span ID**.
2. Every outgoing call **propagates context** in headers — W3C `traceparent: 00-<traceId>-<spanId>-01`.
3. The next service reads the header, creates a **child span** (new span ID, same trace ID, parent = caller's span) and passes its own context onward (HTTP, Kafka headers, gRPC metadata).
4. Each service's tracing SDK **exports** finished spans asynchronously to a collector (OpenTelemetry Collector).
5. The backend (Jaeger, Zipkin, Grafana Tempo) stores spans and **assembles** them by trace ID into a timeline.

**3. Visual**

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant GW as Gateway (span A)
  participant OR as Order service (span B)
  participant PY as Payment service (span C)
  participant COL as OTel Collector → Tempo/Jaeger
  GW->>OR: GET /orders/42  traceparent: 00-abc123-A-01
  OR->>PY: POST /pay  traceparent: 00-abc123-B-01
  PY-->>OR: 200
  OR-->>GW: 200
  GW-->>COL: span A (trace abc123)
  OR-->>COL: span B (parent A)
  PY-->>COL: span C (parent B)
```

**4. Internal implementation**

- Context lives in a thread-local / async context inside each service; instrumentation of HTTP clients, servers, JDBC and messaging creates spans automatically.
- **Sampling** (e.g. 10% of traces, or tail-based: keep slow/error traces) controls cost.
- Trace and span IDs are added to **log lines** (MDC), so logs and traces link together.

**5. Why is it designed this way?**
In microservices, a slow request may be caused by any of a dozen services. Propagating a small context header is cheap and lets a backend rebuild the full call tree without central coordination.

**6. Framework differences**
Spring Boot 3: **Micrometer Tracing** with an OpenTelemetry or Brave bridge (Spring Cloud Sleuth is retired). Java agent: OpenTelemetry Java agent (zero-code). .NET: `System.Diagnostics.Activity` + OpenTelemetry. Node/Python/Go: OpenTelemetry SDKs. Service meshes can create spans at the proxy level.

**7. Practical example**

```properties
management.tracing.sampling.probability=1.0
management.otlp.tracing.endpoint=http://otel-collector:4318/v1/traces
logging.pattern.level=%5p [${spring.application.name},%X{traceId},%X{spanId}]
```

**8. How can I observe it?**
Open the trace in **Jaeger/Zipkin/Grafana Tempo**: a waterfall of spans shows where time is spent. In browser DevTools or `curl -v`, look for the `traceparent` header on outgoing requests; search logs by trace ID.

entries.question: How do Java, JavaScript, Python, Go, Rust and C# implement concurrency differently?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?**
**Concurrency** = handling many tasks that overlap in time; **parallelism** = running them at the same instant on multiple cores. Languages offer very different building blocks: OS threads, lightweight threads, event loops, or ownership-checked threads.

**2. How does it work internally?**

| Language | Unit | Scheduled by | Parallel on many cores? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Java** | Platform `Thread` (1:1 OS thread); **virtual threads** (Java 21, M:N) | OS / JVM scheduler (ForkJoinPool carriers) | Yes |
| **C#** | Threads + `Task` on the thread pool | OS + .NET thread pool | Yes |
| **Go** | **Goroutines** (start ~2 KB stack, growable) | Go runtime **M:N scheduler** (G-M-P model, work stealing) | Yes |
| **Rust** | OS threads (`std::thread`); async tasks via runtimes (Tokio) | OS / Tokio work-stealing scheduler | Yes, with **compile-time** data-race checks |
| **JavaScript** | One thread per realm + **event loop**; Web Workers / `worker_threads` | Engine event loop | Only with workers (no shared objects) |
| **Python (CPython)** | OS threads, but the **GIL** lets one execute Python bytecode at a time; `asyncio`; `multiprocessing` | OS / event loop | Threads: not for Python code (except free-threaded 3.13+ builds); processes: yes |

**3. Visual**

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph J["Java platform threads (1:1)"]
    JT1[Thread] --> OS1[OS thread]
    JT2[Thread] --> OS2[OS thread]
  end
  subgraph G["Go / Java virtual threads (M:N)"]
    G1[goroutine] --> C1[OS thread]
    G2[goroutine] --> C1
    G3[goroutine] --> C2[OS thread]
  end
  subgraph JS["JavaScript"]
    EL["One thread + event loop"] --> Q["task / microtask queues"]
  end
  subgraph PY["CPython"]
    PT1[Thread] --> GIL{GIL}
    PT2[Thread] --> GIL
  end
```

**4. Internal implementation**

- **Shared memory + locks** (Java, C#, C++, Go also has mutexes): need the **memory model** (`volatile`, `synchronized`, atomics) for visibility between cores.
- **Go**: "share memory by communicating" — **channels** pass values between goroutines; the scheduler parks goroutines blocked on I/O and runs others.
- **Rust**: the `Send` and `Sync` traits plus ownership make sharing unsynchronised mutable data a **compile error**.
- **JavaScript**: no shared objects between workers (except `SharedArrayBuffer`) → no data races on normal objects.
- **CPython GIL**: simplifies the interpreter (reference counting isn't thread-safe), at the cost of CPU parallelism for threads.

**5. Why is it designed this way?**
OS threads are general but heavy (~1 MB stack, kernel context switches). M:N lightweight threads make millions of concurrent tasks cheap. Event loops avoid locks entirely but can't use many cores alone. Rust trades compile-time strictness for fearless parallelism.

**6. Language differences**
Covered in the table: the key questions are **1:1 vs M:N**, **shared memory vs message passing**, and **who prevents data races** (you, the compiler, or the single-threaded design).

**7. Practical example**
Handling 10,000 concurrent slow HTTP calls: Java 21 virtual threads or Go goroutines with plain blocking code; Node.js with `Promise.all`; Python with `asyncio.gather`; classic Java platform threads would need 10,000 OS threads.

**8. How can I observe it?**
Java: `jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json out.json` (includes virtual threads). Go: `GODEBUG=schedtrace=1000`, `pprof` goroutine profile. Python: compare CPU-bound threads vs processes timing. Node: `--cpu-prof`, DevTools Performance main-thread view.
entries.summary: What is it? Concurrency = handling many tasks that overlap in time; parallelism = running them at the same instant on multiple cores. Languages offer very different building blocks: OS threads, lightweight threads, event loops, or ownership-checked threads.

entries.question: How do Java, C++, Python and JavaScript create objects internally?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?**
Creating an object means: **allocate memory**, **initialise** its fields, and connect it to its **type** information (for method calls). Each language does these steps differently.

**2. How does it work internally?**

- **Java** `new User("Asha")`:
  1. Class loaded and initialised if first use.
  2. Memory allocated on the heap (TLAB bump pointer), fields **zeroed**.
  3. Object header written (mark word + class pointer).
  4. Constructor chain runs (`super()` first, field initialisers, constructor body).
  5. A reference is returned.
- **C++** `User u("Asha");` / `new User("Asha")`: memory on the **stack** (or heap with `new`), constructor runs; objects with virtual methods get a **vptr** to the class's **vtable**; no header otherwise. Destructor runs at scope end / `delete`.
- **Python** `User("Asha")`: `type.__call__` → `User.__new__` allocates (pymalloc) → `__init__` initialises; every object has a reference count and type pointer; attributes live in a `__dict__` (or fixed `__slots__`).
- **JavaScript** `new User("Asha")`: creates an object whose prototype is `User.prototype`, runs the constructor with `this` bound to it; V8 assigns a **hidden class (map)** and transitions it as properties are added.

**3. Visual**

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Java
    J1[load class] --> J2["allocate (TLAB) + zero"] --> J3[header: mark + class ptr] --> J4["constructor chain"]
  end
  subgraph CPP["C++"]
    C1["stack or heap memory"] --> C2["vptr (if virtual)"] --> C3[constructor]
  end
  subgraph Python
    P1["__new__ (allocate)"] --> P2["refcount + type ptr"] --> P3["__init__ fills __dict__"]
  end
  subgraph JS["JavaScript (V8)"]
    S1["object with prototype"] --> S2["hidden class (map)"] --> S3["constructor sets this.x → map transitions"]
  end
```

**4. Internal implementation**

| | Header / overhead | Method lookup | Layout fixed? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Java | 12–16 bytes header | vtable + inline caches | Yes (class) |
| C++ | 0 bytes (+ vptr if virtual) | Direct call or vtable | Yes |
| Python | ~16 bytes + `__dict__` | Dictionary lookups along the MRO (with caches) | No (unless `__slots__`) |
| JavaScript | Map pointer + properties | Hidden class + inline caches | Dynamic, optimised when shapes are stable |

**5. Why is it designed this way?**
Static languages know the layout at compile time → compact objects and fast field access. Dynamic languages allow adding attributes at runtime, so engines add tricks (hidden classes, `__slots__`) to recover speed.

**6. Language differences**
Covered above. Practical rule: in JavaScript, initialise all properties in the constructor in the same order so objects share hidden classes; in Python, use `__slots__` for millions of small objects.

**7. Practical example**

```java
User u = new User("Asha");   // bytecode: new User; dup; ldc "Asha"; invokespecial User.<init>
```

```js
function P(x, y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }   // all P objects share one hidden class
```

**8. How can I observe it?**
Java: `javap -c` (the `new` / `invokespecial` pair), **JOL** for object size. Python: `sys.getsizeof(obj)`, `obj.__dict__`. V8: `node --allow-natives-syntax` with `%HaveSameMap(a, b)`; DevTools heap snapshot shows object sizes. C++: `sizeof(User)`.

entries.question: How do Spring, ASP.NET Core and Angular implement Dependency Injection differently?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?** All three provide an **IoC container**: you declare dependencies; the framework constructs objects and passes them in. They differ in **when** wiring happens, **object lifetimes**, and how the container is **structured**. **2. How does it work internally?** - **Spring (Java)**: at start-up, scan classes → `BeanDefinition`s → create singletons eagerly, resolving constructor parameters **by type** via reflection; post-processors may wrap beans in proxies. - **ASP.NET Core (C#)**: you register services in `Program.cs` (`AddSingleton/AddScoped/AddTransient`); the `ServiceProvider` builds them **lazily** on first request using constructor parameters; **scoped** services live per HTTP request. - **Angular (TypeScript)**: the compiler generates a factory per injectable; **hierarchical injectors** (environment → element) resolve tokens by walking up the tree at runtime; `providedIn: 'root'` services are lazy and tree-shakable. **3. Visual** ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph Spring S1["Scan @Component / @Bean"] --> S2["BeanDefinitions"] --> S3["Create singletons at start-up
(reflection, proxies)"] end subgraph ASP["ASP.NET Core"] A1["builder.Services.AddScoped: IRepo → Repo"] --> A2["ServiceProvider"] --> A3["Per request scope:
create scoped services lazily"] end subgraph Angular N1["Compiler: factory per @Injectable"] --> N2["Element injector → parent → environment → root"] --> N3["First match creates/returns instance"] end ``` **4. Internal implementation** | | Spring | ASP.NET Core | Angular | |---|---|---|---| | Registration | Annotations + scanning, `@Bean` | Explicit in code | Decorators + `providers` arrays | | Resolution time | Start-up (eager singletons) | First use (lazy) | First injection (lazy) | | Lifetimes | singleton, prototype, request, session | singleton, scoped (request), transient | per injector (root, route, component) | | Mechanism | Reflection (or AOT-generated) | Reflection / compiled expression trees | Compiler-generated factories | | Extra | AOP proxies, conditional auto-config | Middleware, options pattern | Hierarchy per component tree | **5. Why is it designed this way?** Spring favours convention (scanning, auto-configuration) for large enterprise apps; ASP.NET Core favours explicit registration and request scopes; Angular needs a **tree** of injectors to match the UI component tree and lazy-loaded routes. **6. Framework differences** Build-time DI exists too: Dagger/Hilt (Android), Micronaut and Quarkus (Java), which generate wiring code instead of using runtime reflection → faster start-up. **7. Practical example** ```java // Spring @Service class OrderService { OrderService(OrderRepository repo) { } } ``` ```csharp // ASP.NET Core builder.Services.AddScoped(); public class OrderService(IOrderRepository repo) { } ``` ```ts // Angular @Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' }) export class OrderService { private repo = inject(OrderApi); } ``` **8. How can I observe it?** Spring: `/actuator/beans`. ASP.NET Core: `builder.Host.UseDefaultServiceProvider(o => o.ValidateScopes = true)` catches lifetime mistakes; debugger shows the `ServiceProvider`. Angular: DevTools → Injector Tree.
entries.summary: What is it? All three provide an IoC container: you declare dependencies; the framework constructs objects and passes them in. They differ in when wiring happens, object lifetimes, and how the container is structured.

(reflection, proxies)"] end subgraph ASP["ASP.NET Core"] A1["builder.Services.AddScoped: IRepo → Repo"] --> A2["ServiceProvider"] --> A3["Per request scope:
create scoped services lazily"] end subgraph Angular N1["Compiler: factory per @Injectable"] --> N2["Element injector → parent → environment → root"] --> N3["First match creates/returns instance"] end

entries.question: How do Java, JavaScript, Python, C# and Kotlin implement asynchronous execution?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?** **Asynchronous execution** lets a program start slow work (I/O, timers) and continue doing other things, resuming the rest of the code when the result is ready — without blocking a thread while waiting. **2. How does it work internally?** - **JavaScript**: `async/await` compiles to a **state machine** over Promises; continuations run as **microtasks** on the single event-loop thread. - **C#**: `async/await` compiled by Roslyn into a **state machine struct**; awaiting a `Task` registers a continuation; it resumes on the thread pool (or the captured `SynchronizationContext` in UI apps). - **Python**: `async def` creates a **coroutine** (a generator-like object); `await` yields control to the **asyncio event loop**, which uses `selectors` (epoll/IOCP) to resume coroutines when I/O is ready. - **Kotlin**: `suspend` functions are transformed by the compiler into **continuation-passing** state machines; **coroutines** run on dispatchers (thread pools) and are very cheap. - **Java**: `CompletableFuture` chains callbacks on executors; reactive (Project Reactor `Mono/Flux`); since Java 21, **virtual threads** make plain blocking code behave asynchronously under the hood (the JVM unmounts the virtual thread on I/O). **3. Visual** ```mermaid flowchart LR F["async function / suspend fun"] --> SM["Compiler: state machine
state 0 → await → state 1 → ..."] SM --> AW{"await on I/O"} AW -- "not ready" --> SAVE["save locals + state
return to scheduler"] SAVE --> LOOP["Event loop / thread pool
runs other work"] LOOP -- "I/O ready (epoll / IOCP)" --> RES["resume at next state"] AW -- "already done" --> RES ``` **4. Internal implementation** | Language | Await target | Resumes on | Colours functions? | |---|---|---|---| | JavaScript | Promise | Same event-loop thread (microtask) | Yes (`async`) | | C# | Task / ValueTask | Thread pool / sync context | Yes | | Python | Awaitable (coroutine/Future) | asyncio loop thread | Yes | | Kotlin | `suspend` call | Coroutine dispatcher | Yes (`suspend`) | | Java 21 | (none — blocking call on a virtual thread) | Any carrier thread | **No** | "Coloured functions" = async code can only be awaited from async code, which spreads `async` through the codebase; Java's virtual threads (and Go's goroutines) avoid that. **5. Why is it designed this way?** Threads blocked on I/O waste memory; state machines let one thread serve thousands of waiting operations. Languages differ in whether they make this explicit (await) or hide it in the runtime (virtual threads, goroutines). **6. Language differences** See the table. Pitfalls: blocking calls inside async code freeze the event loop (Node, Python); `.Result`/`.Wait()` in C# can deadlock; `synchronized` blocks pinned virtual threads in Java 21–23 (fixed in Java 24). **7. Practical example** ```js const [user, orders] = await Promise.all([getUser(id), getOrders(id)]); // both requests in flight at once ``` ```kotlin val user = async { api.user(id) }; val orders = async { api.orders(id) } show(user.await(), orders.await()) ``` **8. How can I observe it?** Decompile a C# async method (ILSpy/SharpLab.io) or a Kotlin suspend function (IntelliJ "Show Kotlin Bytecode") to see the generated state machine. Node: `--trace-event-categories`. Python: `asyncio` debug mode (`PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1`) warns about slow callbacks.
entries.summary: What is it? Asynchronous execution lets a program start slow work (I/O, timers) and continue doing other things, resuming the rest of the code when the result is ready — without blocking a thread while waiting.

state 0 → await → state 1 → ..."] SM --> AW{"await on I/O"} AW -- "not ready" --> SAVE["save locals + state
return to scheduler"] SAVE --> LOOP["Event loop / thread pool
runs other work"] LOOP -- "I/O ready (epoll / IOCP)" --> RES["resume at next state"] AW -- "already done" --> RES

val user = async { api.user(id) }; val orders = async { api.orders(id) }

entries.question: How do Java, Python, C++, C# and JavaScript implement exception handling internally?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?**
An **exception** transfers control from where an error happens to the nearest matching handler up the call stack, running cleanup code on the way. Languages differ in the **cost model**, **checked vs unchecked** rules, and **cleanup** mechanisms.

**2. How does it work internally?**
General flow:

1. `throw` creates an exception object (often capturing a **stack trace**).
2. The runtime searches the current function for a matching handler (`catch`).
3. None → the function's frame is **unwound** (popped), cleanup runs (`finally`, destructors, `using`), and the search continues in the caller.
4. Found → execution continues in the handler. Not found anywhere → the thread/program terminates with an uncaught-exception error.

**3. Visual**

```mermaid
flowchart BT
  T["parse() throws NumberFormatException"] --> U1["unwind parse(): run finally"]
  U1 --> L["loadConfig(): no matching catch → unwind"]
  L --> M["main(): catch (NumberFormatException e)"]
  M --> H[Handler runs, program continues]
```

**4. Internal implementation**

| Language | Mechanism | Cost when no exception | Cleanup |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Java** | Per-method **exception table** (bytecode ranges → handler) | ~Zero | `finally`, try-with-resources |
| **C#** | Two-pass SEH-style: find handler, then unwind | ~Zero | `finally`, `using` |
| **C++** | **Zero-cost** unwind tables (Itanium ABI / Windows SEH) | Zero; throw is expensive | **Destructors (RAII)** |
| **Python** | Exception table (3.11+ "zero-cost"), unwinds interpreter frames | ~Zero | `finally`, `with` (context managers) |
| **JavaScript** | Engine unwinds the call stack; async errors become **rejected Promises** | ~Zero | `finally` |

- **Checked exceptions** exist only in **Java**: the compiler forces you to catch or declare them. Kotlin, C#, Python and JS have only unchecked ones.
- Filling stack traces is the main throw cost in Java; `new Exception(msg, cause, false, false)` can disable it for control-flow-heavy cases.

**5. Why is it designed this way?**
Table-based ("zero-cost") exceptions make the normal path fast and pay only when something goes wrong — matching how rare errors should be. Go and Rust deliberately avoid exceptions for expected errors, returning error values (`error`, `Result`) so failure paths are explicit.

**6. Language differences**
See the table; plus: C++ `noexcept` functions terminate if they throw; JavaScript `await` turns a rejected Promise back into a thrown error inside `try/catch`; unhandled Promise rejections crash Node.js processes (since Node 15).

**7. Practical example**

```java
try (var in = Files.newBufferedReader(path)) {   // closed automatically, even on exception
    return parse(in.readLine());
} catch (IOException e) {
    throw new ConfigException("Cannot read " + path, e);   // keep the cause
}
```

**8. How can I observe it?**
Java: `javap -c -v` shows the `Exception table:` of a method. IntelliJ / VS / Chrome DevTools: "break on exceptions" (caught and uncaught). C++: Compiler Explorer shows `.gcc_except_table` sections. Python: `dis.dis()` on 3.11+ prints the exception table.
entries.summary: What is it? An exception transfers control from where an error happens to the nearest matching handler up the call stack, running cleanup code on the way. Languages differ in the cost model, checked vs unchecked rules, and cleanup mechanisms.

  U1 --> L["loadConfig(): no matching catch → unwind"]
  L --> M["main(): catch (NumberFormatException e)"]
  M --> H[Handler runs, program continues]

entries.question: Which tools can I use to observe software internals, and what should I look for?
entries.answer:
**1. What is it?** A toolbox for **seeing** what this whole section describes: bytecode, threads, memory, GC, network packets, query plans, containers, caches and messages. Observing real behaviour is how you confirm theory and find problems. **2. How does it work internally?** Tools get information in three ways: 1. **Runtime introspection APIs** — the JVM's JMX / JFR events, V8 inspector protocol, .NET EventPipe. 2. **OS-level instrumentation** — process/thread tables, performance counters, packet capture (Npcap/libpcap), eBPF. 3. **Application/DB statistics** — `EXPLAIN` plans, Redis `INFO`, Kafka metrics, Actuator endpoints. **3. Visual** ```mermaid flowchart LR APP["Your application"] --> RT["Runtime: JFR, JMX, V8 inspector"] APP --> OS["OS: threads, memory, sockets"] APP --> DB["Database / Redis / Kafka stats"] RT --> T1["VisualVM, JDK Mission Control,
IntelliJ debugger, Chrome DevTools"] OS --> T2["Task Manager, Process Explorer,
Wireshark, netstat"] DB --> T3["EXPLAIN, redis-cli, Kafka CLI / UI"] ``` **4. Internal implementation** | Area | Tools | Look for | |---|---|---| | Java / JVM | IntelliJ debugger, VisualVM, JConsole, **JFR + JDK Mission Control**, `javap`, `jcmd` | Hot methods, GC pauses, heap growth, blocked threads, bytecode | | JavaScript / browser | **Chrome DevTools** (Performance, Memory, Network, Sources) | Long tasks > 50 ms, layout thrashing, detached DOM leaks, waterfall | | Angular | **Angular DevTools** | Change detection cycles, component tree, injectors | | Database | `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, SQL Server execution plans + `SET STATISTICS IO ON` | Scans vs seeks, estimated vs actual rows, logical reads | | Networking | **Wireshark**, browser Network tab, `curl -v` | Handshakes, retransmissions, TTFB, protocol (h2/h3) | | Memory | VisualVM heap dump, JFR allocation profiling, Eclipse MAT | Retained size, dominator tree, allocation hot spots | | Operating system | Task Manager, **Process Explorer**, Resource Monitor | Threads per process, handles, page faults, CPU per core | | Docker | `docker stats`, `docker inspect`, Docker Desktop | Memory vs limit, restarts, layers, mounts | | Redis | `redis-cli INFO`, `SLOWLOG`, `MONITOR` | Hit ratio, memory, slow commands | | Kafka | `kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe`, Kafka UI | Consumer lag, partition skew, under-replicated partitions | **5. Why is it designed this way?** Low-overhead, always-on tools (JFR, metrics) let you observe production safely; heavy tools (debuggers, heap dumps, packet capture) are for reproducing issues locally or in staging. **6. Language differences** .NET: `dotnet-counters`, `dotnet-trace`, `dotnet-dump`, Visual Studio diagnostics. Python: `cProfile`, `py-spy`, `tracemalloc`. Go: `pprof`, `go tool trace`. Node: `--inspect` + Chrome DevTools, `clinic.js`. Rust/C++: `perf`, Valgrind, sanitizers. **7. Practical example** "Spring Boot API is slow": JFR recording (method profiling) → most time in `OrderRepository.findAll` → `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` shows a sequential scan → add an index → JFR confirms the hotspot is gone. **8. How can I observe it?** Start small: `jcmd JFR.start duration=60s filename=rec.jfr`, open it in JDK Mission Control; record a page load in Chrome DevTools Performance; capture one HTTPS request in Wireshark; run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` on your slowest query. For each, write down what you expected vs what you saw.

entries.question: Difference between `substring()` and `slice()`?
entries.answer:
Both extract a portion of a string, but they handle **negative numbers and reversed ranges differently**.

```js
// substring() treats negative numbers as 0
"world".substring(-2, 4);     // "worl"  (treated as substring(0, 4))

// slice() counts negative numbers from the end
"world".slice(-2, 4);         // "l"    (start = 5-2 = 3, end = 4)

// substring() swaps args if start > end
"hello".substring(4, 1);      // "ell"  (swapped to substring(1, 4))

// slice() returns empty string if start > end
"hello".slice(4, 1);          // ""     (no swap)
```

| Method        | Negative args     | Reversed args   |
| ------------- | ----------------- | --------------- |
| `substring()` | Treated as 0      | Swapped         |
| `slice()`     | Count from end    | Returns ""      |

> 💡 **Recommendation**: prefer `slice()` — it's more predictable and works on arrays too.

entries.question: Two Sum (LeetCode 1)
entries.prompt:
Given an array `nums` and an integer `target`, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to `target`. Exactly one solution exists, and the same element can't be used twice.

Example: `nums = [2, 7, 11, 15], target = 9` → `[0, 1]`
entries.answer:
**Pattern:** hash map. For each number, check whether its complement (`target - num`) was already seen.

```python
def two_sum(nums: list[int], target: int) -> list[int]:
    seen = {}                        # value -> index
    for i, num in enumerate(nums):
        need = target - num
        if need in seen:
            return [seen[need], i]
        seen[num] = i
    return []

print(two_sum([2, 7, 11, 15], 9))   # [0, 1]
print(two_sum([3, 2, 4], 6))        # [1, 2]
```

**Complexity:** `O(n)` time, `O(n)` space. The brute-force double loop is `O(n²)`.
entries.summary: Pattern: hash map. For each number, check whether its complement (target - num) was already seen.

entries.question: Product of Array Except Self (LeetCode 238)
entries.prompt:
Return an array where `answer[i]` is the product of all numbers except `nums[i]`, without using division, in `O(n)`.

Example: `[1, 2, 3, 4]` → `[24, 12, 8, 6]`
entries.answer:
**Pattern:** prefix and suffix products. First store the product of everything to the left, then multiply by the product of everything to the right.

```python
def product_except_self(nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    n = len(nums)
    result = [1] * n
    prefix = 1
    for i in range(n):
        result[i] = prefix           # product of nums[0..i-1]
        prefix *= nums[i]
    suffix = 1
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        result[i] *= suffix          # times product of nums[i+1..]
        suffix *= nums[i]
    return result
```

**Complexity:** `O(n)` time, `O(1)` extra space apart from the output.
entries.summary: Pattern: prefix and suffix products. First store the product of everything to the left, then multiply by the product of everything to the right.

entries.question: Search Insert Position (LeetCode 35)
entries.prompt:
Given a sorted array of distinct integers and a target, return the index of the target. If it is absent, return the index where it would be inserted to keep the array sorted.

Example: `nums = [1, 3, 5, 6], target = 2` → `1`
entries.answer:
**Pattern:** binary search for the first position whose value is `>= target` (the "lower bound").

```python
def search_insert(nums: list[int], target: int) -> int:
    left, right = 0, len(nums)       # the answer can be len(nums)
    while left < right:
        mid = (left + right) // 2
        if nums[mid] < target:
            left = mid + 1           # answer is to the right of mid
        else:
            right = mid              # mid may be the answer
    return left

print(search_insert([1, 3, 5, 6], 5))  # 2 (found)
print(search_insert([1, 3, 5, 6], 2))  # 1 (insert between 1 and 3)
print(search_insert([1, 3, 5, 6], 7))  # 4 (insert at the end)
print(search_insert([1, 3, 5, 6], 0))  # 0 (insert at the start)
```

Python's standard library does the same: `bisect.bisect_left(nums, target)`.

**Complexity:** `O(log n)` time, `O(1)` space.
entries.summary: Pattern: binary search for the first position whose value is >= target (the "lower bound").

entries.question: Container With Most Water (LeetCode 11)
entries.prompt:
Given wall heights, choose two walls that hold the most water: `width × min(height)`.

Example: `[1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7]` → `49`
entries.answer:
**Pattern:** two pointers at both ends. Always move the **shorter** wall inward — moving the taller one can never increase the area.

```python
def max_area(height: list[int]) -> int:
    left, right = 0, len(height) - 1
    best = 0
    while left < right:
        best = max(best, (right - left) * min(height[left], height[right]))
        if height[left] < height[right]:
            left += 1
        else:
            right -= 1
    return best
```

**Complexity:** `O(n)` time, `O(1)` space.
entries.summary: Pattern: two pointers at both ends. Always move the shorter wall inward — moving the taller one can never increase the area.

entries.question: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters (LeetCode 3)
entries.prompt:
Return the length of the longest substring with no repeated characters.

Example: `"abcabcbb"` → `3` (`"abc"`)
entries.answer:
**Pattern:** sliding window. Remember where each character was last seen; when a character repeats inside the window, move the window's start past it.

```python
def length_of_longest_substring(s: str) -> int:
    last_seen = {}                   # character -> last index
    start = best = 0
    for i, ch in enumerate(s):
        if ch in last_seen and last_seen[ch] >= start:
            start = last_seen[ch] + 1
        last_seen[ch] = i
        best = max(best, i - start + 1)
    return best

print(length_of_longest_substring("abcabcbb"))  # 3
print(length_of_longest_substring("pwwkew"))    # 3
```

**Complexity:** `O(n)` time, `O(k)` space for `k` distinct characters.
entries.summary: Pattern: sliding window. Remember where each character was last seen; when a character repeats inside the window, move the window's start past it.

**Pattern:** keep a min-heap of the `k` largest values seen; its smallest element is the answer.

```python
import heapq

def find_kth_largest(nums: list[int], k: int) -> int:
    heap = []
    for num in nums:
```

entries.question: Reverse a Linked List (LeetCode 206)
entries.prompt: Reverse a singly linked list and return the new head.
entries.answer:
Walk the list once, turning each `next` pointer backwards.

```python
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next

def reverse_list(head: ListNode | None) -> ListNode | None:
    prev = None
    while head:
        nxt = head.next      # remember the rest of the list
        head.next = prev     # reverse this pointer
        prev = head
        head = nxt
    return prev
```

**Complexity:** `O(n)` time, `O(1)` space.

entries.question: Merge Two Sorted Lists (LeetCode 21)
entries.prompt: Merge two sorted linked lists into one sorted list.
entries.answer:
A dummy head avoids special cases for the first node.

```python
def merge_two_lists(a: ListNode | None, b: ListNode | None) -> ListNode | None:
    dummy = tail = ListNode()
    while a and b:
        if a.val <= b.val:
            tail.next, a = a, a.next
        else:
            tail.next, b = b, b.next
        tail = tail.next
    tail.next = a or b       # attach whatever remains
    return dummy.next
```

**Complexity:** `O(n + m)` time, `O(1)` space.
entries.summary: A dummy head avoids special cases for the first node.

entries.question: Linked List Cycle (LeetCode 141)
entries.prompt: Return `True` if the linked list has a cycle.
entries.answer:
**Pattern:** Floyd's fast and slow pointers. If there is a cycle, the fast pointer eventually meets the slow one.

```python
def has_cycle(head: ListNode | None) -> bool:
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
        if slow is fast:
            return True
    return False
```

**Complexity:** `O(n)` time, `O(1)` space.

entries.question: Number of Islands (LeetCode 200)
entries.prompt: Given a grid of `"1"` (land) and `"0"` (water), count the islands (groups of land connected up, down, left or right).
entries.answer:
**Pattern:** DFS flood fill. When you find land, count an island and "sink" all land connected to it.

```python
def num_islands(grid: list[list[str]]) -> int:
    rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])

    def sink(r, c):
        if r < 0 or c < 0 or r >= rows or c >= cols or grid[r][c] != "1":
            return
        grid[r][c] = "0"             # mark as visited
        sink(r + 1, c)
        sink(r - 1, c)
        sink(r, c + 1)
        sink(r, c - 1)

    count = 0
    for r in range(rows):
        for c in range(cols):
            if grid[r][c] == "1":
                count += 1
                sink(r, c)
    return count
```

**Complexity:** `O(rows × cols)` time and space. For very large grids, use BFS with `collections.deque` to avoid Python's recursion limit.
entries.summary: Pattern: DFS flood fill. When you find land, count an island and "sink" all land connected to it.

entries.question: Climbing Stairs (LeetCode 70)
entries.prompt:
You can climb 1 or 2 steps at a time. How many distinct ways are there to reach step `n`?

Example: `n = 3` → `3` (1+1+1, 1+2, 2+1)
entries.answer:
Ways to reach step `n` = ways to reach `n-1` + ways to reach `n-2` — the Fibonacci pattern.

```python
def climb_stairs(n: int) -> int:
    a, b = 1, 1              # ways to reach the previous two steps
    for _ in range(n - 1):
        a, b = b, a + b
    return b

print(climb_stairs(5))       # 8
```

**Complexity:** `O(n)` time, `O(1)` space.

entries.question: Maximum Subarray (LeetCode 53)
entries.prompt:
Find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum.

Example: `[-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]` → `6` (`[4, -1, 2, 1]`)
entries.answer:
**Pattern:** Kadane's algorithm. At each number, either extend the current subarray or start a new one there.

```python
def max_sub_array(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    best = current = nums[0]
    for num in nums[1:]:
        current = max(num, current + num)
        best = max(best, current)
    return best
```

**Complexity:** `O(n)` time, `O(1)` space.
entries.summary: Pattern: Kadane's algorithm. At each number, either extend the current subarray or start a new one there.

entries.question: Write a country-wise order analytics query (orders, highest/lowest/average amount, unique customers, orders between 1000 and 5000)
entries.prompt:
> Given a `customer` table and an `orders` table:
>
> - total number of orders per country
> - highest and lowest order amount per country
> - average order value per country
> - number of unique customers per country
> - number of orders with amount greater than 1000 and less than 5000
> - sorted by country name
entries.answer:
```sql
SELECT
    c.country,
    COUNT(o.order_id)              AS total_orders,
    MAX(o.order_amount)            AS highest_order_amount,
    MIN(o.order_amount)            AS lowest_order_amount,
    AVG(o.order_amount)            AS average_order_value,
    COUNT(DISTINCT c.customer_id)  AS total_customers,
    SUM(CASE WHEN o.order_amount > 1000 AND o.order_amount < 5000 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
                                   AS orders_between_1000_and_5000
FROM customer c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
GROUP BY c.country
ORDER BY c.country;
```

🧠 **How it works:** the join gives one row per order with its customer's country; `GROUP BY` makes one result row per country; each aggregate summarises that country's orders. The `SUM(CASE ...)` trick counts only the rows that match a condition.

> 💡 `JOIN` skips customers with no orders. To include them (with 0 orders), use `LEFT JOIN` — `COUNT(o.order_id)` then correctly gives 0.

entries.question: What is the output of `WHERE salary = NULL`?
entries.answer:
**No rows** — even if some salaries are NULL.

🧠 **Why:** `NULL` means "unknown". `salary = NULL` is never true (it's unknown), so no row passes.

✅ Correct:

```sql
SELECT * FROM employee WHERE salary IS NULL;
```
entries.summary: No rows — even if some salaries are NULL.

entries.question: What is the difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(column)?
entries.answer:
- `COUNT(*)` → counts **all rows**.
- `COUNT(salary)` → counts rows where `salary` is **not NULL**.

Example: 5 employees, 2 without a salary → `COUNT(*) = 5`, `COUNT(salary) = 3`.
entries.summary: COUNT(*) → counts all rows. COUNT(salary) → counts rows where salary is not NULL.

codeBlocks.code: SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(salary) FROM employee;

entries.question: How do you find the second highest salary?
entries.answer:
```sql
-- 1. Subquery: highest salary below the maximum
SELECT MAX(salary) AS second_highest
FROM employee
WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employee);

-- 2. LIMIT / OFFSET — DISTINCT is required
SELECT DISTINCT salary
FROM employee
ORDER BY salary DESC
LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1;
```

> ⚠️ **Trap:** without `DISTINCT`, if two people share the top salary, query 2 returns the **top salary again**.

For the Nth highest, `DENSE_RANK()` is the cleanest — see the SQL interview queries notes.

entries.question: How do you find duplicate records?
entries.answer:
```sql
SELECT name, COUNT(*) AS copies
FROM employee
GROUP BY name
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
```

🧠 **How:** group rows by the column(s) that define a duplicate, then keep groups with more than one row. `HAVING` filters groups (after `GROUP BY`); `WHERE` can't use `COUNT(*)`.

entries.question: EXISTS vs IN — what's the difference?
entries.answer:
Both find employees in the IT department:

```sql
-- IN: is dept_id in this list of values?
SELECT name
FROM employee
WHERE dept_id IN (SELECT id FROM department WHERE dept_name = 'IT');

-- EXISTS: does at least one matching row exist?
SELECT e.name
FROM employee e
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM department d WHERE d.id = e.dept_id AND d.dept_name = 'IT'
);

-- Both return: Asha, Meena
```

| `IN` | `EXISTS` |
|---|---|
| Compares a value with a **list** | Checks whether **any row** matches |
| Natural for small, fixed lists: `IN (1, 2, 3)` | Natural for "has related rows" checks |
| `NOT IN` breaks if the list contains **NULL** | `NOT EXISTS` is safe with NULLs |

**Performance:** modern MySQL (8.0+) and PostgreSQL usually turn both into the same plan (a semi-join), so speed is normally similar. The real difference is **`NOT IN` vs `NOT EXISTS`**:

```sql
-- If any department id were NULL, this returns NO rows at all
SELECT name FROM employee WHERE dept_id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM department);
```

✅ Prefer `NOT EXISTS` for "not in another table" checks.

entries.question: | Frameworks / Libraries |
entries.answer:
- [![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-20232A?style=flat&logo=react&logoColor=61DAFB)](https://reactjs.org)
  * #### Development Server:
      * webpack-dev-server – used in older setups (like Create React App).
      * Vite – used in modern setups, faster due to native ES modules and esbuild.
  * #### Production Server:
      * Node.js, Nginx, Apache, or cloud services like Vercel, Firebase, or Netlify.
  * #### Transpiler & Compiler:
      * React uses **Babel** to transpile JSX into plain JavaScript, which the browser can execute directly.
      * No need for a separate compiler — Everything runs in the browser using the JavaScript engine with the help of the Virtual DOM.
  * #### DOM Updation:
      * React updates the UI by using a **Virtual DOM** and a process called **reconciliation** to efficiently compare changes between renders and update only what’s necessary.

- [![Angular](https://img.shields.io/badge/Angular-DD0031?style=flat&logo=angular&logoColor=white)](https://angular.io)
  * #### Development Server:
      * webpack-dev-server under the hood, configured by Angular CLI.
  * #### Production Server:
      * Node.js, Nginx, Apache, or cloud services like Vercel, Firebase, or Netlify.
  * #### Transpiler & Compiler:
      * Angular uses the **Ivy compiler** first to process decorators and compile templates into JavaScript.
      * Then, the **TypeScript compiler (tsc)** transpiles into final JavaScript.
      * During development, Ivy uses a JIT (Just-in-Time) strategy to compile templates in the browser for faster rebuilds.
      * During production, Ivy uses an AOT (Ahead-of-Time) strategy to compile everything at build time for optimized performance.
  * #### DOM Updation:
      * Angular works with the real DOM, using **zone.js** to track asynchronous operations and automatically trigger **change detection**, which then scans the component tree to detect state changes and updates the UI accordingly.

entries.question: Career Hierarchy: Individual Contributor (Technical) Track
entries.answer:
| Level | Title | Also called | Typical years | Scope |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| L1 | Intern / Trainee | Graduate Trainee, Apprentice | 0 | Learns basics; works on small, guided tasks. |
| L2 | Junior / Associate Software Engineer | SE I, Programmer Analyst | 0–2 | Delivers well-defined tasks with code review and guidance. |
| L3 | Software Engineer | SE II, Developer | 2–4 | Owns features end-to-end inside one team; works independently. |
| L4 | Senior Software Engineer | SE III, Sr. Developer | 4–8 | Owns components, designs solutions, mentors juniors, handles production issues. |
| L5 | Lead / Tech Lead | Lead Engineer, Module Lead | 6–10 | Sets technical direction for a team; splits work, reviews designs, unblocks people. |
| L6 | Staff Engineer | Senior Lead, Technical Architect | 8–12+ | Solves problems spanning multiple teams; drives standards and large designs. |
| L7 | Principal Engineer / Architect | Solution / Enterprise Architect | 12–15+ | Shapes architecture across an organisation; long-term technical strategy. |
| L8 | Distinguished Engineer / Fellow | Chief Architect | 15+ | Company-wide or industry-level technical influence. |
entries.summary: L1: Intern / Trainee; L2: Junior / Associate Software Engineer; L3: Software Engineer; L4: Senior Software Engineer; L5: Lead / Tech Lead; L6: Staff Engineer; L7: Principal Engineer / Architect; L8: Distinguished Engineer / Fellow

entries.question: Career Hierarchy: Management (People) Track
entries.answer:
| Level | Title | Also called | Typical years | Scope |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | Engineering Manager | Project Manager (service cos.) | 7–10+ | Manages one team: hiring, 1:1s, delivery, performance. |
| M2 | Senior Engineering Manager | Delivery Manager, Program Manager | 10–14+ | Manages several teams or managers; owns delivery of a product area. |
| M3 | Director of Engineering | Associate Director, Head of Engineering | 12–18+ | Owns a department; budgets, org design, cross-team strategy. |
| M4 | VP of Engineering | Senior Director | 15+ | Runs engineering execution for the whole company or business unit. |
| M5 | CTO / CIO | Chief Technology / Information Officer | 15–20+ | Owns technology vision (CTO) or internal IT systems (CIO); reports to CEO. |

- IC = Individual Contributor (technical track). M = Management (people track). Both tracks pay similarly at equal levels.
- Titles and years vary by company. Product companies use L-levels; service companies (TCS, Infosys, Accenture…) use titles like Associate → Senior → Lead → Manager → Senior Manager → AVP → VP.
- Switching between tracks is common around Senior/Lead level.
- Parallel ladders exist for QA, DevOps, Data, Design and Product — same shape: Junior → Mid → Senior → Lead → Principal/Head.
entries.summary: IC = Individual Contributor (technical track). M = Management (people track). Both tracks pay similarly at equal levels. Titles and years vary by company. Product companies use L-levels; service companies (TCS, Infosys, Accenture…) use titles like Associate → Senior → Lead → Manager → Senior Manager → AVP → VP.…

entries.question: What does a Forward Deployed Engineer do?
entries.answer:
Engineer embedded with a customer to build and deploy the company's product (often AI) into the customer's real systems.

- **Also called:** Forward Deployed Software Engineer, Deployment Strategist, Solutions Engineer (AI), Field Engineer
- **At IT services firms (TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Accenture):** AI Solutions Consultant / Implementation Lead
- **At product / Big Tech companies:** FDE (Palantir, OpenAI, Anthropic, Scale AI)
- **At startups:** Founding / Customer Engineer
- **Typical experience to be hired:** 3+ yrs
- **Next moves — grow:** AI Solutions Architect, Tech Lead · **lead:** Engineering Manager · **pivot:** AI Product Manager, Solutions / Sales Engineer
- **Why it exists now:** Popularised by Palantir; now hired by OpenAI, Anthropic, Scale AI and AI startups because enterprise AI only creates value once wired into messy real-world data and workflows.
- **Languages:** Python, TypeScript, SQL, Java/Go (varies)
- **Frameworks / Standards:** LLM SDKs (Claude, OpenAI), FastAPI, React/Next.js, MCP, LangGraph, Palantir Foundry/AIP
- **Tools:** AWS/Azure/GCP, Docker, Git, Jupyter, Postman, Customer data platforms
- **Technical skills:** Rapid prototyping, Full-stack development, Data integration & ETL, API integration with legacy systems, RAG & agent building, Debugging in customer environments, Solution scoping, Deployment & security reviews
- **Soft skills:** Customer discovery, Executive communication, Ownership, Comfort with ambiguity, Travel / on-site work
- **AI impact:** Core of AI go-to-market — turns a model into a working customer solution.
entries.summary: Engineer embedded with a customer to build and deploy the company's product (often AI) into the customer's real systems.

entries.question: What does an AI Agent Engineer do?
entries.answer:
Builds autonomous AI agents that plan, call tools and complete multi-step tasks.

- **Also called:** Agentic AI Engineer, LLM Application Engineer, AI Workflow Engineer
- **At IT services firms (TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Accenture):** GenAI Developer / Agentic AI Consultant
- **At product / Big Tech companies:** Software Engineer, Applied AI / Agents
- **At startups:** AI Engineer
- **Typical experience to be hired:** 2+ yrs
- **Next moves — grow:** AI / LLM Engineer, AI Solutions Architect · **lead:** Engineering Manager · **pivot:** Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE), AI Evaluation (Evals) Engineer
- **Narrower (sideways) roles:** Context / Prompt Engineer, AI Automation Engineer
- **Why it exists now:** LLMs gained reliable tool calling (2024–26), so companies now automate whole workflows, not single prompts.
- **Languages:** Python, TypeScript, Java
- **Frameworks / Standards:** LangGraph, Claude Agent SDK, OpenAI Agents SDK, CrewAI, AutoGen, Spring AI, MCP, A2A protocol
- **Tools:** Claude / GPT / Gemini APIs, Vector DBs, Langfuse / LangSmith, Temporal, Redis
- **Technical skills:** Tool / function calling, Agent planning & memory, Multi-agent orchestration, State management, Error handling & retries, Human-in-the-loop design, Guardrails, Cost & latency control, Agent evaluation
- **Soft skills:** Systems thinking, Risk awareness, Product sense
- **AI impact:** AI-native role — exists because of agentic AI.
entries.summary: Builds autonomous AI agents that plan, call tools and complete multi-step tasks.

entries.question: What does a Context / Prompt Engineer do?
entries.answer:
Designs the prompts, instructions, examples and retrieved context an AI model sees.

- **Also called:** Prompt Engineer, Context Engineer, LLM Prompt Designer
- **At IT services firms (TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Accenture):** GenAI Prompt Specialist
- **At product / Big Tech companies:** Applied AI Engineer (prompting & retrieval)
- **At startups:** AI Engineer
- **Typical experience to be hired:** 1+ yrs
- **Next moves — grow:** AI Agent Engineer, AI / LLM Engineer · **lead:** — · **pivot:** AI Evaluation (Evals) Engineer, Conversational AI Designer
- **Why it exists now:** Output quality depends heavily on context; prompt engineering has grown into 'context engineering' (what data, tools and memory to feed the model).
- **Languages:** Python, Markdown, JSON / YAML
- **Frameworks / Standards:** RAG, Few-shot prompting, Chain-of-thought, Structured outputs (JSON Schema), DSPy
- **Tools:** Model playgrounds / Workbench, promptfoo, Langfuse, Vector DBs
- **Technical skills:** Prompt design & versioning, Context window management, Retrieval tuning, Output formatting, Prompt testing & A/B, Prompt-injection defence, Domain knowledge capture
- **Soft skills:** Clear writing, Experimentation mindset, Attention to detail
- **AI impact:** Increasingly merged into AI Engineer and Agent Engineer roles.
entries.summary: Designs the prompts, instructions, examples and retrieved context an AI model sees.

entries.question: What does an AI Evaluation Engineer do?
entries.answer:
Measures whether AI outputs are correct, safe and improving between versions.

- **Also called:** LLM Evaluation Engineer, AI Quality Engineer, Model Evaluation Scientist
- **At IT services firms (TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Accenture):** GenAI Test / Quality Engineer
- **At product / Big Tech companies:** Research Engineer, Evals / Applied AI Quality
- **At startups:** AI Engineer (evals)
- **Typical experience to be hired:** 2+ yrs
- **Next moves — grow:** AI / LLM Engineer, AI Red Teamer / AI Safety Engineer · **lead:** Engineering Manager · **pivot:** Machine Learning Engineer, Responsible AI / AI Governance Lead
- **Why it exists now:** AI output is non-deterministic; teams need automated tests ('evals') before shipping model or prompt changes.
- **Languages:** Python, SQL
- **Frameworks / Standards:** Ragas, DeepEval, OpenAI Evals, LLM-as-judge, Inspect
- **Tools:** Braintrust, LangSmith, Langfuse, promptfoo, Weights & Biases
- **Technical skills:** Test-set (golden dataset) design, Metrics: accuracy, groundedness, relevance, LLM-as-judge setup, Regression tracking, Statistics, Human review workflows, Error analysis
- **Soft skills:** Critical thinking, Rigor, Communication of results
- **AI impact:** AI-native role — the 'QA' of AI systems.
entries.summary: Measures whether AI outputs are correct, safe and improving between versions.

entries.question: What does an AI Red Teamer / AI Safety Engineer do?
entries.answer:
Attacks and stress-tests AI systems to find harmful, unsafe or insecure behaviour.

- **Also called:** AI Red Team Specialist, Trust & Safety Engineer (AI), Adversarial ML Engineer
- **At IT services firms (TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Accenture):** AI Security Consultant
- **At product / Big Tech companies:** Red Team / Safety Research Engineer
- **At startups:** AI Security Engineer
- **Typical experience to be hired:** 3+ yrs
- **Next moves — grow:** Responsible AI / AI Governance Lead, Application Security (AppSec) / DevSecOps Engineer · **lead:** — · **pivot:** Penetration Tester / Ethical Hacker, Cloud Security Engineer
- **Why it exists now:** Prompt injection, jailbreaks and data leakage are new attack types; regulation (EU AI Act) requires testing.
- **Languages:** Python
- **Frameworks / Standards:** OWASP Top 10 for LLMs, MITRE ATLAS, NIST AI RMF
- **Tools:** Garak, PyRIT, promptfoo, Guardrails AI, NeMo Guardrails
- **Technical skills:** Jailbreak & prompt-injection testing, Data-leakage testing, Bias & toxicity testing, Agent tool-abuse testing, Writing safety evals, Mitigation design, Reporting findings
- **Soft skills:** Adversarial mindset, Ethics, Clear reporting
- **AI impact:** AI-native security role.
entries.summary: Attacks and stress-tests AI systems to find harmful, unsafe or insecure behaviour.
keywords: ai red teamer / ai safety engineer
names: AI Red Teamer / AI Safety Engineer

entries.question: What does an AI Product Manager do?
entries.answer:
Decides which AI features to build and how to measure their value and risks.

- **Also called:** Product Manager – AI/ML, GenAI Product Owner, ML Product Manager
- **At IT services firms (TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Accenture):** AI Product Owner / Business Consultant (AI)
- **At product / Big Tech companies:** Product Manager, AI Platform / Applied AI
- **At startups:** Product Lead (AI)
- **Typical experience to be hired:** 4+ yrs
- **Next moves — grow:** — · **lead:** CTO / CIO · **pivot:** Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE), AI Solutions Architect
- **Narrower (sideways) roles:** Product Owner (PO)
- **Why it exists now:** AI products need different decisions: model choice, accuracy targets, cost per request, safety and user trust.
- **Languages:** SQL (basic), Python (helpful)
- **Frameworks / Standards:** Agile, OKRs, AI evaluation basics, Responsible AI
- **Tools:** Jira, Claude / ChatGPT, Model playgrounds, Amplitude, Figma
- **Technical skills:** AI use-case discovery, Model capability & limits, Defining eval metrics, Cost / latency trade-offs, Prototyping with no-code AI, Data requirements, AI UX patterns, Roadmapping
- **Soft skills:** Stakeholder management, Storytelling, Prioritisation
- **AI impact:** AI-native PM specialisation.
entries.summary: Decides which AI features to build and how to measure their value and risks.

entries.question: What does an AI Solutions Architect do?
entries.answer:
Designs end-to-end AI systems — models, data, RAG, agents, security and cost.

- **Also called:** GenAI Architect, AI/ML Solutions Architect, AI Technical Architect
- **At IT services firms (TCS, Infosys, Wipro, Accenture):** GenAI Architect / AI CoE Architect
- **At product / Big Tech companies:** Solutions Architect – AI/ML (cloud vendors)
- **At startups:** Head of AI Engineering
- **Typical experience to be hired:** 8+ yrs
- **Next moves — grow:** Enterprise Architect · **lead:** CTO / CIO · **pivot:** Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE), AI Product Manager
- **Why it exists now:** Enterprises need someone to choose between models, cloud AI services and build-vs-buy options.
- **Languages:** Python, Java/TypeScript

entries.question: Expected Pay Abroad (typical software engineer, by experience)
entries.answer:
Estimates from public salary surveys and job ads for a typical software engineer, shifted by role. Gross pay before tax unless marked tax-free; cost of living differs a lot — compare take-home, rent and schooling before deciding. The ₹ figure uses an approximate exchange rate and is only for comparison.

| Country | Period | 0–2 yrs | 2–5 yrs | 5–8 yrs | 8–12 yrs | 12+ yrs | Tax |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Germany | per year (EUR) | 45,000–56,000 | 55,000–68,000 | 65,000–82,000 | 75,000–95,000 | 85,000–110,000 | gross |
| UAE (Dubai/Abu Dhabi) | per month (AED) | 9,000–14,000 | 14,000–21,000 | 19,000–28,000 | 23,000–34,000 | 30,000–45,000 | tax-free |
| Netherlands | per year (EUR) | 40,000–50,000 | 50,000–62,000 | 60,000–76,000 | 70,000–90,000 | 80,000–105,000 | gross (30% ruling may apply) |
| Ireland | per year (EUR) | 40,000–52,000 | 55,000–70,000 | 65,000–85,000 | 80,000–105,000 | 95,000–130,000 | gross |
| Remote for global companies | per year (USD) | 15,000–30,000 | 25,000–45,000 | 40,000–65,000 | 55,000–90,000 | 70,000–120,000 | gross, paid to you in India |
| Japan | per year (JPY) | 4,000,000–5,500,000 | 5,500,000–7,500,000 | 7,000,000–9,500,000 | 8,500,000–12,000,000 | 10,000,000–15,000,000 | gross |
| Australia | per year (AUD) | 75,000–95,000 | 95,000–125,000 | 120,000–150,000 | 140,000–175,000 | 160,000–200,000 | gross, plus 11.5% super |
| United Kingdom | per year (GBP) | 32,000–42,000 | 42,000–58,000 | 55,000–75,000 | 70,000–95,000 | 85,000–120,000 | gross (London ~15% higher) |
| Singapore | per month (SGD) | 4,500–6,500 | 6,000–9,000 | 8,500–12,000 | 11,000–16,000 | 14,000–20,000 | gross, low income tax |
